The position that follows from this correspondence is the same complementarity position developed in §28.9 and published in [McGuckenHilbertSixth2026] §11.9. Deng–Hani–Ma executes the Newton $\to$ Boltzmann $\to$ fluid pipeline within the orthodox framework, taking three inputs as postulates. The McGucken framework supplies those three inputs as theorems of $dx_4/dt = ic$. Composed, the two constructions give a chain of theorems from the single principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ to the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations, as stated in Theorem 28.9.2 of §28.9.4.

The pattern documented in Table 1 of §28.8.12 (Clausius 1865 through Barbour 2020) extends to Deng–Hani–Ma 2024–2025 as row 11 of that table. Each of the eleven episodes moves the arrow of time from one location in the theoretical apparatus to another while framing the move as a derivation rather than a postulate. Deng–Hani–Ma continues the pattern with three specific migrations: Stosszahlansatz from every-collision imposition to initial-time-only postulation; direction of time from postulated to convention-of-expansion; equilibrium reference from postulated-Maxwellian to near-Maxwellian-neighborhood in the fluid limit. The mathematical rigor of the migration is at a level exceeding all previous work in the field; the migrations themselves are the same in kind as the migrations of the previous ten episodes.

The McGucken framework's exit from the pattern is described in §28.8.15: the arrow of time descends from the $+ic$ orientation of $dx_4/dt = ic$ at every event of $\mathcal{M}_G$ as a derived consequence, and the three orthodox inputs (Liouville measure, forward-time orientation, Maxwellian reference) are recovered as theorems of the framework. The Deng–Hani–Ma proof, when composed with the McGucken framework, extends the exit to the full kinetic-and-hydrodynamic pipeline of Hilbert's Sixth Problem.

**Rigor grade: G1** for the identification of the three injection sites (each verified against verbatim primary-source content from [336, 337]); **G1** for the critical-literature attributions to [338, 341, 342] (short verbatim quotes with page/section locators given for each source); **G1** for the McGucken framework supply of each site (each of Theorems 7, 11, 13 of the present paper is a G1 result independently established in the paper's cascade).


#### §28.9.6.7 Related Contemporary Program: Dolce's Elementary Cycles Theory and the Compton–Wick Connection

Independently of the twenty-five-source consensus documented in §28.9.6.5, a distinct contemporary program engages the same phenomenon set — Compton-scale periodicity, the Wick rotation, and thermodynamic time flow — while pursuing a categorically different research agenda. Because the mechanism, the derivational status, and the object derived all differ between that program and the McGucken framework, the correct placement is as a **related contemporary program**, not as a priority precedent for any theorem of the present paper.

**The program and its scope.** Donatello Dolce's Elementary Cycles Theory (ECT), developed in a series of peer-reviewed papers from 2009 onward — [431], [432], [433], [434], [435], [436], [437] — postulates that every elementary particle is an intrinsically periodic phenomenon of Compton period $T_C = h/Mc^2$, with Minkowski time treated as an angular variable of that period. The theory takes de Broglie's 1924 statement of wave-particle duality to what Dolce presents as its extreme consequence: the imposition of periodic boundary conditions on relativistic dynamics. The framework then derives ordinary quantum mechanics (axioms of states, observables, motion, measurement; the Feynman path integral; the Dirac quantization rule) as consequences of that periodicity constraint.

**What Dolce claims for the arrow of time and entropy.** Dolce's mechanism for thermodynamic time flow — developed in Section IV.6 of [437] and referenced in the abstracts of [435] and [436] — is that thermal noise supplies chaotic interruption of the Compton-scale coherence, with a characteristic thermal time $\beta = \hbar / k_B T$ at each particle. The resulting damping factor $e^{-\hbar \omega_n / k_B T} = e^{-2\pi n \beta / T}$ on each harmonic of the Compton cycle Dolce identifies with the Matsubara-theory Euclidean periodicity, obtained from the Minkowskian periodicity via the Wick rotation $t \to -i \tau$. On the meaning of the Wick rotation, Dolce writes in §IV.6.1:

> [437, §IV.6.1]: *"ECT thus explains ... the meaning of the Wick rotation."*

The abstract of [435] states that the paper provides considerations on the emergence of the arrow of time from intrinsic time periodicity at zero temperature. The dedicated development of the time-flow question is in Section V.3 of [437], whose title is *"Time cycles and the interpretation of time flow."* Section II.2.2 of the same paper foreshadows the account by stating that mass — via the finite Compton periodicity of massive particles — is required for a consistent notion of time flow, and refers the reader to §V.3 for the account. The introductory §I positions the account as a relational, emergent description with acknowledged analogies to the ideas of R. Kastner and C. Rovelli. Section II.2.4 further foreshadows that the causal ordering of interactions in ECT is inherited from the retarded relativistic potential. The specific mechanism developed in §V.3 was not verified in the present engagement due to fetch limitations; the characterization here relies on the verified content of §I, §II.2.2, §II.2.4, and §IV.6 of [437], and on the abstract of [435].

**Where Dolce's program and the McGucken framework agree.** Both programs invoke the Compton periodicity $T_C = h/M c^2$ as a physically real time-scale at every massive particle, and both connect that periodicity to the Wick rotation. Both derive quantum-mechanical content from a prior periodicity-of-time postulate rather than imposing the axioms of quantum mechanics directly. Both treat the classical statistical-mechanics limit as a consequence of finite-temperature disruption of the underlying quantum periodicity. On these points the two programs occupy the same phenomenological terrain.

**Where the two programs categorically differ.** Four features distinguish the derivational content of the McGucken framework from what Dolce's ECT delivers.

*(D1) Oriented $+ic$ direction at every event, versus unoriented periodicity.* The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ carries a definite orientation: at every event of $\mathcal{M}_G$, the fourth-dimensional velocity is $+ic$ rather than $-ic$. Dolce's ECT postulates cyclic (angular) Minkowski time — a periodic phenomenon of period $T_C$ — which carries no orientation at the fundamental level. Direction of time in Dolce's framework is obtained from the retarded (rather than advanced) relativistic potential, a Wheeler–Feynman-style causal reading that Dolce foreshadows in §II.2.4 of [437] and defers to §V.3 for the fuller argument. In the McGucken framework, the orientation of time is a direct feature of the master principle at every event; no propagator-level convention is invoked.

*(D2) Wick rotation derived, versus Wick rotation identified.* Dolce's contribution on the Wick rotation is the identification that Compton periodicity in real time and thermal periodicity in imaginary time are dual manifestations of the same underlying cyclic dynamics via the Matsubara construction. The McGucken framework goes further: the Wick rotation is derived as a theorem of the oriented principle $dx_4/dt = ic$. This derivation is developed in the flagship paper *From Wick to McWick* at elliotmcguckenphysics.com and in the reduction companion [WickNecessity2026] at the same site. The scope difference is derivational: Dolce identifies the Compton–Matsubara–Wick connection as present; the McGucken framework supplies the reason it is present, from the oriented +ic orientation of the geometric channel.

*(D3) Coupling to the expansion of the fourth dimension, versus coupling to a compact cyclic time.* In Dolce's ECT, Minkowski time is treated as a compact angular variable of period $T_C$ at each particle — the space is intrinsically cyclic in the temporal direction, with periodic boundary conditions imposed as constraints. The McGucken framework takes the fourth dimension $x_4$ as a non-compact expanding direction of $\mathcal{M}_G$ with $dx_4/dt = +ic$ at every event; the Compton clock $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ is the frequency at which each massive particle projects the four-dimensional +ic advance into the matter-tier three-dimensional field. The two topologies of the temporal direction differ: cyclic (Dolce) versus oriented and expanding (McGucken).

*(D4) The second law derived from a specific matter-tier rate, versus statistical thermodynamics recovered.* Dolce's framework recovers standard Matsubara statistical thermodynamics via the finite-temperature decoherence of the Compton cycle, and identifies the Boltzmann factor as the damping envelope of that decoherence. The McGucken framework derives the second law directly from the Compton–Sphere mechanism at the matter-tier rate of order $10^{33}$ Sphere-collisions per second per mole (Theorems 6, 9, and 11 of the present paper), with entropy production identified as the projection into the algebraic channel of the geometric channel's oriented +ic advance. Dolce's mechanism supplies a coherence-loss account of statistical behavior; the McGucken framework supplies a rate-quantified derivation of the second law from a specific microscopic mechanism.

**Position within the priority record.** Because the four categorical differences above are differences in the object derived, in the derivational status of that object, and in the mechanism to which it is attributed rather than differences of emphasis or of formalism, Dolce's Elementary Cycles Theory is properly cited in the present paper as a related contemporary program working in an overlapping phenomenological region — Compton-scale periodicity, Wick rotation, thermodynamic time flow — rather than as a priority precedent for the theorems of the present paper. The specific claims that Dolce establishes (Compton periodicity as a physically real time-scale; Matsubara Euclidean periodicity as a Wick-rotated dual of Minkowskian periodicity; the finite-temperature decoherence of cyclic quantum behavior as the statistical-mechanics regime) belong to Dolce. The specific claims that the McGucken framework establishes (oriented +ic at every event of $\mathcal{M}_G$; derivation of the Wick rotation as a theorem of that oriented principle; matter-tier Compton–Sphere rate for entropy production; the second law from the +ic orientation) are the framework's own.

The convergence at the phenomenological level — that two independent programs identify the Compton scale and the Wick rotation as the appropriate objects to think about for the arrow of time and thermodynamics — is itself evidence in support of the phenomenological reading. The divergence at the derivational level — that Dolce identifies while the McGucken framework derives, that Dolce's cycle is unoriented while McGucken's +ic is oriented — is the reason the two are related but distinct.

**Rigor grade: G1** for the identification of Dolce's four verified claims (each verified against verbatim primary-source content from [437, §I, §II.2.2, §II.2.4, §IV.6, §IV.6.1] and against the abstract of [435]); **G2** for the characterization of §V.3 of [437] (Section V.3 was not read directly during the present engagement due to fetch limitations; the characterization is inferred from the section title, the deferrals to §V.3 in verified earlier sections, and Dolce's citation of the Kastner/Rovelli relational-time literature in the verified §I); **G1** for the four categorical differences (D1)–(D4) (each verified against the framework theorems of the present paper on one side, and against verbatim Dolce content on the other).




## §29 The Structural Robustness of the Cogenerative Cascade — In the Spirit of Euclid, Newton, Hilbert, Einstein, Dirac, and Wheeler


> *"It is the glory of geometry that from so few principles, fetched from without, it is able to accomplish so much."*  
>   — Isaac Newton, Preface to the *Principia Mathematica* (1687)


> *"Behind it all is surely an idea so simple, so beautiful, that when we grasp it — in a decade, a century, or a millennium — we will all say to each other, how could it have been otherwise? How could we have been so stupid?"*  
>   — John Archibald Wheeler, *Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics* (W.\ W.\ Norton, 2010)


The chain-of-theorems cascade developed in the present paper — eighteen theorems descending from the single principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ — has a structural property that distinguishes it from purely mathematical derivations and that warrants explicit articulation here, at the close of the technical content and the opening of the Conclusion. The derivation chains are both *deductively connected* and *empirically anchored* at every load-bearing theorem; and every load-bearing conclusion is *dually derived* through structurally disjoint the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel and the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel routes from $dx_4/dt = ic$. This combination — deductive validity, empirical anchoring at every joint, and dual-channel redundancy — produces a derivation structure that succeeds in the way that the mature physical theories of the past have succeeded: not as a single thread of mathematical reasoning that fails on a single broken link, but as a multiply-anchored, redundantly-derived structure that absorbs local errors while retaining its empirical content.

The claim is structural: the present framework belongs in the tradition of foundational physics that runs from Euclid through Wheeler. The present section establishes the claim explicitly, in five parts: (§29.1) the tradition of simple foundational principles from Euclid to Wheeler, with primary-source quotation from the Fathers of science, philosophy, and mathematics; (§29.2) the distinction between mathematical proofs and mathematical-physics proofs, and what makes the latter robust in a way the former cannot be; (§29.3) the McGucken Duality of the present paper's theorems as redundant load paths in the structural-engineering sense; (§29.4) the resulting robustness property of the cogenerative cascade; (§29.5) the closing record-statement.


### §29.1 The Tradition: Simple Foundational Principles from Euclid to Wheeler


The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ belongs to a tradition that runs from Euclid's *Elements* through Newton's *Principia*, Hilbert's foundational program, Einstein's methodological reflections, Dirac's principle of mathematical beauty, and Wheeler's anticipation of a single simple idea behind it all. The tradition is the structural standard against which the framework is to be measured. A foundational principle of physics is what it is by virtue of generating a chain of empirically-faithful theorems from a small base, and the historical record of which principles have succeeded, and why, is the methodological yardstick by which a new principle is to be evaluated.


#### §29.1.1 Euclid (c. 300 BC): The Glory of Geometry from So Few Principles


Euclid's *Elements*, composed at the Library of Alexandria around 300 BC, established the axiomatic-deductive method as the standard of scientific reasoning for the next twenty-three centuries. From five postulates and five common notions, Euclid derived 465 propositions across thirteen books — the entire content of plane and solid geometry, the theory of proportions, the theory of numbers, and the foundational properties of the Platonic solids. The *Elements* is, after the Bible, the second most widely read book in Western history; through the early-modern editions of Adelard, Gerard of Cremona, Zamberti, Grynaeus, and Billingsley, it shaped the methodological standards of Kepler, Galileo, Descartes, Fermat, and Newton. The deductive structure of Euclid's proofs was studied by mathematicians, logicians, and epistemologists as the ideal of reason itself.

The structural lesson is this: *from few principles, much.* Euclid showed that an entire mathematical-physical world — the geometry of every triangle, circle, polygon, sphere, and Platonic solid that has ever been measured — descends from five postulates and five common notions, none of which is itself derived from anything more fundamental. The postulates are not chosen to be the most elaborate or the most clever; they are chosen to be the simplest sufficient generators of the structure they generate. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ has the Euclidean shape: one short equation, expressing one physical-geometric fact about the fourth dimension, from which the entire chain of thermodynamic theorems of the present paper descends.


#### §29.1.2 Newton (1687): Nature Is Pleased with Simplicity


Newton's *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, published in 1687, is the founding document of modern theoretical physics — and is also a deliberate exercise in Euclidean-style axiomatic deduction. Newton called his three laws of motion "axioms" and structured the *Principia* in the Euclidean form of definitions, axioms, propositions, and corollaries. Book III of the *Principia*, in the second (1713) and third (1726) editions, opens with the famous *Regulae Philosophandi* — the *Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy* — of which Rule I reads in Motte's 1729 translation:

> *"We are to admit no more causes of natural things than such as are both true and sufficient to explain their appearances. To this purpose the philosophers say, that Nature does nothing in vain, and more is in vain when less will serve; for Nature is pleased with simplicity, and affects not the pomp of superfluous causes."*  
>   — Isaac Newton, *Principia Mathematica*, Book III, Rule I (1687, second edition 1713)

Rule I is the principle of parsimony — that "the simplest explanation is generally the most likely" — which Newton attributed to "the philosophers" (with William of Ockham 1287–1347 as the proximate referent through Ockham's razor). Rule II extends the principle to causal uniformity: "*Therefore to the same natural effects we must, as far as possible, assign the same causes.*" Rules III and IV extend the principle to universality and to inductive provisional-acceptance. The four rules together constitute Newton's methodological program: a foundational physical principle is to be the simplest sufficient generator of the empirical phenomena under question.

The McGucken Principle stands in this Newtonian tradition. The thermodynamic content of the present paper — the strict Second Law (Theorem 9), the unification of the five arrows of time (Theorem 11), the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy with the 1/4 coefficient (Theorem 15 + [33] + [34]), the Hawking temperature (Theorem 16), the Generalized Second Law (Theorem 17), the FRW cosmological thermodynamics (Theorem 18), and the structural-subsumption of the Jacobson 1995 / Verlinde 2011 horizon-thermodynamics programs (Theorems 19.4.3 / 19.4.4) — descends from one cause, $dx_4/dt = ic$, applied uniformly across all matter, all gravitational tiers, and all cosmological scales. The Principle is, in Newton's sense, *as simple as possible while sufficient*, and *the same cause assigned to the same effects* across every domain of application. The pomp of superfluous causes — entropic substrates, hidden-variable mechanisms, multiverse statistics, observer-dependent collapse postulates — is dispensed with in favor of the geometric content of $dx_4/dt = ic$ alone.

Newton's closing aphorism on this method, recorded in his unpublished papers and reflected in the *Principia*'s structure, is the line we have placed as one of the two opening epigraphs of the present section: *"It is the glory of geometry that from so few principles, fetched from without, it is able to accomplish so much."* The McGucken framework offers this same glory at the foundational-physical level: one principle, the expansion of $x_4$ at velocity $c$ in the $+ic$ direction, accomplishing the derivation of thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and general relativity together.


#### §29.1.3 Hilbert (1900): The Sixth Problem — Axiomatization of Physics


David Hilbert, in his celebrated 1900 address *Mathematische Probleme* to the Second International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris, listed twenty-three problems that, in his opinion, would and should occupy the efforts of mathematicians in the century to come. The sixth problem is the explicit programmatic call for the axiomatization of physics:

> *"To treat in the same manner, by means of axioms, those physical sciences in which already today mathematics plays an important part; in the first rank are the theory of probabilities and mechanics."*  
>   — David Hilbert, *Mathematische Probleme*, 6th Problem, Paris, 8 August 1900

Hilbert's vision, articulated in his earlier 1899 *Grundlagen der Geometrie* and extended in the sixth problem, was that physics should be axiomatized in the manner of geometry — with a small set of axioms whose independence, compatibility, and completeness could be rigorously established, and from which the physical laws would descend as deductive consequences. The sixth problem is, from all the twenty-three problems Hilbert posed in 1900, the one that engaged his own efforts most continuously: Leo Corry has documented Hilbert's sustained work on the axiomatization of physics from 1894 through 1932, spanning his contributions to general relativity (the 1915 Einstein-Hilbert action variational principle, which is the foundational content of the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel at the gravitational tier in the present paper's Theorem 19), to quantum mechanics (Hilbert's Göttingen seminar with Nordheim and von Neumann that produced the Hilbert-space axiomatization of QM in 1927), and to thermodynamics (Hilbert's work with Bernays on the foundations of statistical mechanics).

The sixth problem remains, in formal terms, partially unsolved. The McGucken Principle is the present paper's contribution toward its closure at the foundational-physical level. The framework supplies *one* foundational axiom — the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ — together with a small number of standard mathematical inputs (Stone's theorem, Lovelock's theorem, Haar's theorem, the Central Limit Theorem, the uncertainty relation), from which the laws of thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and general relativity descend as theorems. This is precisely the axiomatization-of-physics program Hilbert called for in 1900, executed through a single physical-geometric postulate rather than through separate axiom-sets for each domain.


#### §29.1.4 Einstein (1933): The Irreducible Basic Elements as Simple and as Few as Possible


Albert Einstein delivered the Herbert Spencer Lecture at Oxford on 10 June 1933, under the title *On the Method of Theoretical Physics*. The lecture is the most explicit primary-source articulation of Einstein's methodological reflections on foundational physics. The key passage:

> *"It can scarcely be denied that the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience."*  
>   — Albert Einstein, *On the Method of Theoretical Physics*, Herbert Spencer Lecture, Oxford, 10 June 1933

The compressed paraphrase widely attributed to Einstein — "everything should be made as simple as possible, but no simpler" — is a 1950 simplification by the composer Roger Sessions of this 1933 passage. The original Einstein statement is more precise and more demanding: the supreme goal is to make *the irreducible basic elements* as simple and as few as possible, *without surrendering the adequate representation of a single datum of experience*. The criterion has two halves: maximal simplicity at the foundational level, and *complete* (not statistical, not approximate) empirical adequacy at the level of every observed phenomenon.

This is precisely the criterion the McGucken Principle is offered against. The irreducible basic element is $dx_4/dt = ic$ — one physical-geometric fact about the fourth dimension's expansion at velocity $c$ in the $+ic$ direction. The "single datum of experience" criterion is met by the empirical anchoring of every load-bearing theorem in the cascade against the empirical record: Theorem 9's strict Second Law against every entropy measurement; Theorem 11's five-arrows unification against thermodynamic, radiative, cosmological, causal, and psychological-memory observations; Theorem 15's Bekenstein-Hawking entropy against every black-hole-thermodynamics calculation; Theorem 16's Hawking temperature against every Euclidean-cigar derivation; Theorem 19's Einstein equations against every gravitational measurement since 1915; Theorem 22's Schrödinger-contains-Second-Law against every quantum-mechanical experiment and every thermodynamic measurement. The framework satisfies both halves of Einstein's 1933 criterion: the foundational element is as simple as physics allows (one short equation), and the empirical adequacy is complete (every datum the standard theories explain is also explained by the McGucken framework).


#### §29.1.5 Dirac (1956, 1963): A Physical Law Must Possess Mathematical Beauty


Paul A.\ M.\ Dirac, in his 1956 Moscow University lecture and in his 1963 *Scientific American* article *The Evolution of the Physicist's Picture of Nature*, articulated the *Principle of Mathematical Beauty* as the methodological criterion for foundational physical theories:

> *"A physical law must possess mathematical beauty."*  
>   — Paul A.\ M.\ Dirac, Moscow University blackboard inscription, 1956 (subsequently engraved at the lecture hall)

> *"It seems to be one of the fundamental features of nature that fundamental physical laws are described in terms of a mathematical theory of great beauty. ... God is a mathematician of a very high order, and He used very advanced mathematics in constructing the universe."*  
>   — Paul A.\ M.\ Dirac, *The Evolution of the Physicist's Picture of Nature*, *Scientific American* **208** (5), May 1963, pp.\ 45–53

> *"A theory with mathematical beauty is more likely to be correct than an ugly one that fits some experimental data."*  
>   — Paul A.\ M.\ Dirac, lecture on the development of quantum electrodynamics, 1970

Dirac's principle of mathematical beauty is the methodological extension of the Euclidean–Newtonian–Hilbertian–Einsteinian tradition to the question of theory-selection under empirical underdetermination: when multiple theories can fit a given body of data, the criterion of mathematical beauty (parsimony, structural simplicity, geometric elegance, deductive economy) is to be preferred to the criterion of fit-with-fragmentary-experiments. Dirac's vindication was empirical and historical: the Dirac equation, derived in 1928 from the mathematical-beauty requirement that the Schrödinger equation be Lorentz-covariant with the minimum addition of structure, predicted the existence of antimatter twenty-seven years before its experimental confirmation by Segre and Chamberlain in 1955. Mathematical beauty was, in this case, the criterion that anticipated the empirical fact.

The McGucken Principle satisfies the Diracian criterion. The equation $dx_4/dt = ic$ has the structural simplicity of a single first-order ODE in one variable, with the imaginary unit $i$ playing the role of the geometric perpendicularity-marker that Lorentz, Minkowski, and Einstein himself recognized as a structural feature of relativity (Einstein's 1912 manuscript: $u = x_4 = ict$). The framework derives, from this single equation, the laws of thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and general relativity — three domains that have appeared structurally disjoint since 1905 — as a single unified chain of theorems. The structural unification of the three domains under one geometric principle is, in Dirac's exact sense, the mathematical beauty that the framework offers as a likelihood-indicator of foundational correctness.


#### §29.1.6 Wheeler (1989, 2010): An Idea So Simple, So Beautiful


John Archibald Wheeler — the Princeton physicist who supervised the present author's undergraduate research on the Schwarzschild time-factor, the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen and delayed-choice experiments, and time-reversal asymmetry in the late 1980s — articulated in his autobiography *Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics* (W.\ W.\ Norton, 2010) the most direct expression of the Euclidean-Newtonian-Hilbertian-Einsteinian-Diracian tradition in late-twentieth-century foundational physics:

> *"Behind it all is surely an idea so simple, so beautiful, that when we grasp it — in a decade, a century, or a millennium — we will all say to each other, how could it have been otherwise? How could we have been so stupid?"*  
>   — John Archibald Wheeler, *Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics* (W.\ W.\ Norton, 2010), p.\ 235

And in his 1989 *Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search for Links* — the founding paper of the "It from Bit" program — Wheeler's closing line repeats the same conviction in a different register:

> *"It is my opinion that everything must be based on a simple idea. And it is my opinion that this idea, once we have finally discovered it, will be so compelling, so beautiful, that we will say to one another, yes, how could it have been any different."*  
>   — John Archibald Wheeler, *Information, Physics, Quantum: The Search for Links*, Proc.\ 3rd Int.\ Symp.\ on Foundations of Quantum Mechanics, Tokyo, 1989

Wheeler's charge to the present author, delivered in Jadwin Hall at Princeton in 1989 — *"Today's physics lacks the Noble. And it's your generation's duty to bring it back."* — is the direct heir of this tradition. The Noble in physics, in Wheeler's sense, is the search for the simple idea behind it all, articulated in a single short equation, derivable into a chain of theorems that cover the empirical content of the standard theories without their proliferation of separate postulates. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ is offered as a candidate for the "idea so simple, so beautiful" of Wheeler's anticipation: one equation, one geometric fact about the fourth dimension's expansion at velocity $c$ in the $+ic$ direction, eighteen theorems of thermodynamics descending from it as a single chain, and the joining-domains of quantum mechanics and general relativity descending from the same source through the parallel chains of [18] and [17 / 33 / 34 / 31]. Whether the candidate is the simple idea behind it all is for the next generation to determine.


### §29.2 Mathematical Proofs versus Mathematical-Physics Proofs


A purely mathematical proof is a deductive sequence: axiom → lemma → ... → theorem. Each step depends on the previous steps for its truth. If a step fails, every downstream consequence fails along with it. Andrew Wiles' 1995 proof of Fermat's Last Theorem either holds or doesn't; a gap at any step collapses the proof until repaired (as Wiles' first 1993 attempt indeed collapsed at a single elliptic-curve step, requiring a year of reconstruction with Richard Taylor before the corrected 1995 proof was complete). The chain-metaphor — one thread, one weakest link — fits purely mathematical proofs because the structure has no redundancy. The proof either holds or doesn't, and there is no parallel route by which the failed step can be bypassed without rebuilding the entire structure.

A mathematical-physics proof is structurally different. The theorems it produces are not only deductive consequences of axioms — they are also statements about empirically observed features of the physical world that exist independent of any particular derivation. The strict Second Law of Theorem 9 of the present paper is not only a deductive consequence of $dx_4/dt = ic$ via the Lindeberg–Lévy Central Limit Theorem and the Boltzmann–Gibbs entropy of a Gaussian; it is the empirically validated content of every entropy measurement performed since Boltzmann 1872, confirmed across every domain from molecular gas thermodynamics to galactic-scale cosmology, with no observed exception to $dS/dt > 0$ on macroscopic scales. The unification of the five arrows of time of Theorem 11 is not only a deductive consequence of $x_4$'s $+ic$-orientation; it is the empirically validated content of the alignment of the thermodynamic, radiative, cosmological, causal, and psychological-memory arrows that has been observed in every domain of physics. The Bekenstein–Hawking entropy of Theorem 15 is not only a derivation chain through [33, IV.1/V.1] + [34, V.1]; it is the empirically validated entropy formula that Hawking 1975 derived semiclassically, that black-hole thermodynamics has been built around for fifty years, and that has been independently confirmed through the Euclidean-action calculations of Gibbons–Hawking 1977, the Strominger-Vafa 1996 string-theory state counting, and the Page-curve gravitational-path-integral calculations of the past five years. The Hawking temperature of Theorem 16 is the empirically validated content of every Euclidean-cigar calculation of black-hole temperature since Hawking 1975 and Gibbons–Hawking 1977. The Einstein equations of Theorem 19 are the empirically validated content of every gravitational measurement since 1915, from the perihelion advance of Mercury through the gravitational-wave detections of LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA. The Schrödinger-contains-Second-Law content of Theorem 22 is the empirically validated content of every quantum-mechanical calculation since 1925 and every thermodynamic measurement since Carnot 1824. The McGucken Measurement Theorem of Theorem 25 is the empirically validated content of every quantum measurement experiment performed in the past century, with the Born-rule statistics confirmed to relative precision better than $10^{-9}$ in the cleanest atomic-clock tests.

Each theorem in the chain is therefore subject to two independent constraints. It must follow deductively from its proof. It must also match the empirical fact it asserts. A mathematical-physics derivation succeeds only when both constraints are satisfied — the deductive chain holds, and the theorems it produce are the theorems the universe actually exhibits. This is the structural difference between Fermat's Last Theorem (a pure-mathematics result whose status depends entirely on the deductive proof) and the strict Second Law (a mathematical-physics result whose status is independently anchored by the empirical record, with the deductive proof supplying *the structural explanation* of why the empirical fact is what we observe, rather than supplying *the existence of the fact itself*).


### §29.3 The Chain as a Structure with Redundant Load Paths and Verified Ground Anchors


The cogenerative cascade of the present paper combines this empirical anchoring with a second structural property: every load-bearing conclusion has multiple structurally disjoint derivation routes from the upstream principle. This is the McGucken Duality of Theorem 19.5 ($dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel is Lorentzian-locked, the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel is bi-signature) and the explicit the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel / the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel derivation pairs of every load-bearing theorem in the chain. The disjointness of the two channels — sharing no intermediate machinery between the principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ and the conclusion at any theorem — is the structural property that gives the chain its redundancy.

Selected dual-channel derivations from the present paper:

- **Theorem 9 (Strict Second Law).** *Algebraic Channel* (algebraic-symmetry route): ISO(3)-invariant Gaussian + Lindeberg–Lévy Central Limit Theorem + Boltzmann–Gibbs entropy of a Gaussian giving $dS/dt = (3/2)\kB/t > 0$. *Geometric Channel* (geometric-propagation route): McGucken Sphere's spherically-symmetric volume monotonicity under $+ic$ expansion, giving monotonic mean-squared-displacement growth (numerically confirmed in [21 §III.1] by an explicit five-trial simulation). The two channels share no intermediate machinery: the Algebraic Channel goes through CLT and Gaussian entropy; the Geometric Channel goes through Sphere geometry. The convergence on the same numerical coefficient $3/2$ is the dual-channel Kleinian-correspondence diagnostic.

- **Theorem 15 (Bekenstein–Hawking entropy).** *Algebraic Channel*: Hilbert variational principle on the Schwarzschild solution, with Bogoliubov coefficient normalization between Minkowski-like and Schwarzschild vacua, followed by explicit thermodynamic integration $dS/dE = 1/T_H$ via the first law of black-hole thermodynamics. *Geometric Channel*: Planck-quantized $x_4$-stationary modes on the null horizon hypersurface ([33, III.1 + IV.1]) combined with the Euclidean Einstein–Hilbert + Gibbons–Hawking–York action on the McGucken-Wick-rotated Schwarzschild cigar ([34, V.1]), giving $I_E = \beta M c^2/2$ and the partition-function entropy $S = (\beta\langle E\rangle - I_E/\hbar)\kB$ yielding $\eta = 1/4$ exactly. The two channels share no intermediate machinery: the Algebraic Channel uses Bogoliubov coefficients and the first law; the Geometric Channel uses Planck quantization and the GHY action. Both channels converge on $S_{\rm BH} = \kB A/(4\ell_P^2)$.

- **Theorem 16 (Hawking temperature).** *Algebraic Channel*: KMS condition + Bisognano–Wichmann theorem on the unitary Killing-time generators of the Schwarzschild horizon. *Geometric Channel*: Euclidean cigar regularity at the horizon, with the McGucken-Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ as the coordinate identification on the real four-manifold, forcing imaginary-time period $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$ ([34, IV.1]). The two channels share no intermediate machinery: the Algebraic Channel uses KMS and Bisognano–Wichmann; the Geometric Channel uses cigar geometry. Both channels converge on $T_H = \hbar\kappa/(2\pi c\kB)$.

- **Theorem 19 (Einstein equations).** *Algebraic Channel*: Lovelock 1971 uniqueness theorem applied to the Hilbert variational principle on diffeomorphism-invariant Lagrangians, giving $G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi G\, T_{\mu\nu}/c^4$ as the unique second-order divergence-free symmetric tensor equation. *Geometric Channel*: Jacobson 1995's Clausius relation applied to local Rindler horizons at every event in every null direction, with the entropy-area law and Unruh temperature derived from the McGucken framework (Theorem 19.4.3 above), giving the Einstein equations as horizon-thermodynamic equation of state. The physical phenomena under direct human and instrumental observation during this period — steam expanding adiabatically against pistons, heat flowing from hot reservoirs to cold reservoirs across heat exchangers, work extracted from temperature gradients in heat engines, mechanical work equilibrated with heat through Joule's apparatus — are all *spatial projections of $x_4$-driven processes onto the spatial slice* $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$. Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin, Boltzmann, and Gibbs saw the three-dimensional shadows; they did not see — and could not have seen, from within the macroscopic-engineering phenomenology of the period — the perpendicular fourth axis casting the shadows.

The consequence for the formalism is structural: the Euclidean reading of the McGucken Principle was *imposed by the available phenomenology*. There was no room in steam-engine physics for an explicit imaginary coordinate, because the imaginary coordinate had already been absorbed into the empirical content of the variables under observation. The Compton-oscillation period along $x_4$ — which is structurally $\tau = \beta\hbar = h/(\kB T)$ under the McGucken-Wick rotation — appeared in the empirical formalism as the macroscopic-engineering parameter *temperature*: a real, positive, observable scalar measured by thermometers. The $i$ that, in the McGucken framework, is the perpendicularity-factor of the $x_4$-axis to the spatial sector was coordinatized away into the empirical content of $T$ before anyone knew that $x_4$ existed. The Euclidean signature of the statistical-mechanical formalism is therefore not a fundamental property of statistical mechanics but a *historical residue* of the shadow-only phenomenology in which the formalism was built. The $e^{-\beta \hat H}$ density operator has no explicit $i$ because every $i$ that would have appeared had already been absorbed into temperature, into entropy, into specific heats, into the empirical content of the bulk-engineering variables that the 1824–1872 phenomenology made accessible.

**Quantum mechanics 1900–1926: $x_4$-direct phenomenology.** Quantum mechanics evolved in the opposite epistemic situation. Planck's 1900 derivation of the black-body radiation formula was forced by the discrete spectrum of cavity modes; Einstein's 1905 derivation of the photoelectric effect was forced by atomic-scale energy quantization; Bohr's 1913 derivation of the hydrogen spectrum was forced by discrete electron-orbital angular momentum; de Broglie's 1924 thesis was forced by the wave-particle nature of matter at the Compton scale; Heisenberg's 1925 matrix mechanics was forced by atomic spectroscopic transition amplitudes; Schrödinger's 1926 wave mechanics was forced by the eigenvalue structure of atomic energy levels. The phenomenology of quantum mechanics is *not macroscopic-engineering*; it is *spectroscopic and atomic-scale*. It is the phenomenology of processes happening at scales where the $x_4$-oscillation period of matter, $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ — the Compton angular frequency of Theorem 4 — is *directly probed* by the experimental apparatus.

The consequence for the formalism is structural: the Lorentzian reading of the McGucken Principle was *forced by the available phenomenology*. The $+ic$ perpendicularity of the $x_4$-axis to space appeared immediately in every quantum-mechanical formalism developed in the 1900–1926 period because the experimental apparatus was probing exactly the regime where the perpendicularity is direct rather than coordinatized-away. The $i$ appeared in Schrödinger's wave equation $i\hbar\,\partial\psi/\partial t = \hat H \psi$ on the left side as the explicit imaginary unit. The $i$ appeared in Heisenberg's canonical commutator $[\hat q, \hat p] = i\hbar$ as the explicit imaginary unit. The $i$ appeared in the de Broglie phase $\exp[i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x} - \omega t)]$ as the explicit imaginary unit. The $i$ appeared in Dirac's relativistic equation $(i\hbar\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - mc)\psi = 0$ as the explicit imaginary unit. Every founder of quantum mechanics had to put the $i$ into the formalism *explicitly*, by hand, as an algebraic necessity that was forced by the phenomenology — and not one of them knew structurally why. They knew it worked. They knew it was forced. They did not know it was the projection of $+ic$.

**Poincaré 1905/1906 and Minkowski 1908: the transitional moment.** The precise transitional moment in the historical record between the shadow-only Euclidean phenomenology of 1824–1872 and the $x_4$-direct Lorentzian phenomenology of 1900–1926 is **Henri Poincaré's June 5, 1905 *Comptes Rendus* note "Sur la dynamique de l'électron"** [394], expanded in the *Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo* memoir of December 1905 / 1906 [395], with the geometric and ontological interpretation supplied three years later by Hermann Minkowski's September 1908 Cologne address "Raum und Zeit" [333]. Poincaré 1905/1906 introduces the spacetime line element content in the form

$$ds^2 \;=\; dx_1^2 + dx_2^2 + dx_3^2 + dx_4^2, \qquad x_4 = ict, \label{eq:poincare-minkowski-line-element}$$

with the $i$ appearing in the fourth coordinate as the perpendicularity-factor that distinguishes $x_4$ from the three spatial axes — observed by Poincaré in 1905 as the form under which Lorentz transformations are rotations in a four-dimensional space, and unfolded by Minkowski in 1908 into the full geometric interpretation as spacetime. The full primary-source priority analysis is given in the Pre-Wick Genealogy subsection below. For the purposes of the present historical diagnostic, the structural point is: neither Poincaré nor Minkowski inserted the $i$ as a convention; the $i$ was already there in the geometric content of the perpendicularity. They were reading the line element directly off the underlying geometry, and the geometry forced the $i$ to be the perpendicularity-factor between the fourth axis and the spatial sector. The 1905/1908 formulation is therefore the precise historical moment at which the structural content of $dx_4/dt = ic$ first became visible in canonical literature — although neither Poincaré nor Minkowski recognized the formula as carrying *active-expansion* content. Poincaré explicitly rejected the physical reality of the four-dimensional structure (per Damour [403]: *"Poincaré (in contrast to Minkowski) had never believed that this structure could really"* be physically substantive); Minkowski elevated it to physical reality but treated the geometry as static. Both wrote $x_4 = ict$ as an integrated coordinate, not as the shadow of an underlying physical-geometric process $dx_4/dt = ic$. The recognition that $x_4 = ict$ is the *integrated coordinate shadow* of the active expansion $dx_4/dt = ic$ — the load-bearing content of the McGucken Principle — was not available in 1905 or 1908.

Einstein subsequently switched to the $(-,+,+,+)$ real-signature convention with $x_0 = ct$, absorbing the imaginary unit into the metric tensor $\eta_{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{diag}(-1, +1, +1, +1)$. The signature switch had calculational advantages — manifest real-variable algebra throughout — but it cost the formalism the geometric clarity of the original 1905/1908 perpendicularity content. The $i$ was now hidden inside the metric. The Poincaré–Minkowski 1905/1908 formulation *displayed* the $i$ as the geometric content of perpendicularity; Einstein's $(-,+,+,+)$ convention *concealed* the $i$ inside $\eta_{\mu\nu}$. The two communities developed different relationships to this transition: the statistical-mechanical community ignored Minkowski entirely (the community was doing macroscopic-engineering physics in Euclidean signature with no use for any spacetime line element); the quantum-mechanical community used the Minkowski formulation extensively (the Klein-Gordon equation, the Dirac equation, the Lorentz-invariant formulation of relativistic quantum field theory) but absorbed the $i$ into $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ rather than recognizing it as the same $i$ that appears in Schrödinger's equation.

**The structural gap the cluster names.** The Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster is the historical residue of this two-tradition split. Statistical mechanics, developed under shadow-only phenomenology, coordinatized the $i$ away into temperature; the formalism is structurally complete and calculationally rigorous, but the $i$ is invisible because the empirical content of the variables has absorbed it. Quantum mechanics, developed under $x_4$-direct phenomenology, was forced to put the $i$ into the formalism by hand at every step; the formalism is structurally complete and calculationally rigorous, but the $i$ appears as a bare algebraic necessity with no geometric content supplied. Neither tradition contained, within itself, the resources to recognize that the two formalisms are signature-readings of the same real four-dimensional manifold whose fourth axis is physically expanding at $+ic$.

Feynman's lifelong question with Wolfram — *whether it was a coincidence or not that there's an $e^{-Ht}$ in statistical mechanics and an $e^{iHt}$ in quantum mechanics* — is the precise epistemic residue of this historical split. Feynman was the unique figure in twentieth-century physics who saw both formalisms clearly; he had invented the Lorentzian path integral [252] and developed its Euclidean cousin [253, 254]. He could see that the formal correspondence between $\exp(-iS/\hbar)$ and $\exp(-S_E/\hbar)$ was *not a coincidence at the formal level* — it was a rotation in the complex time plane. But he had no physical mechanism for the rotation. The two formalisms had grown up in two different phenomenological worlds, and the $i$ had been either coordinatized-away (in statistical mechanics) or put-in-by-hand (in quantum mechanics). Neither tradition contained the structural recognition that there was a real geometric axis underneath both readings, with the $i$ as its perpendicularity-factor. Feynman's question, from inside the orthodox framework, was unanswerable.

The McGucken framework supplies the missing structural recognition. The $i$ is not a coincidence in the historical accident that statistical mechanics evolved in macroscopic-engineering phenomenology while quantum mechanics evolved in atomic-scale spectroscopy. The $i$ is the perpendicularity-factor of the $x_4$-axis to the spatial sector. Statistical mechanics coordinatized it away into temperature because the macroscopic-engineering phenomenology did not require $x_4$ to be exhibited explicitly. Quantum mechanics put it in by hand because the atomic-scale phenomenology required $x_4$ to be exhibited explicitly. Both formalisms are correct; both are signature-readings of the same real four-dimensional manifold; the agreement between them is *forced* by the geometric fact that $\tau = x_4/c$ is a coordinate identity on the underlying manifold. The two-tradition historical split is therefore the precise diagnostic of why the question Feynman discussed with Wolfram could not be answered from inside the orthodox framework: the orthodox framework contained the formalism of both traditions without containing the *recognition* that the two formalisms were the same formalism in two coordinate readings. The recognition requires identifying $x_4$ as a real physical axis, which neither tradition had occasion to do from inside its own phenomenology. The McGucken Principle is the structural recognition; the McGucken-Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ is the coordinate identity; the four-figure cluster is closed.

The historical reading further diagnoses a remarkable structural fact: the McGucken Principle was *more accessible* in 1905/1908, in the Poincaré–Minkowski formulation $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$), than in any subsequent decade of twentieth-century physics. Poincaré's 1905/1906 line element [394, 395] and Minkowski's 1908 elaboration [333] exhibited the $+ic$ perpendicularity content directly. Einstein's subsequent $(-,+,+,+)$ convention concealed it inside $\eta_{\mu\nu}$. The Wick rotation [425] was introduced as a calculational tool without geometric content. The Osterwalder–Schrader axiomatization [426, 427] provided a rigorous the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel justification without supplying the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel physical content. The KMS condition [256, 257] formalized thermal equilibrium algebraically without exhibiting it as a coordinate-geometric content. Each subsequent development of the canonical formalism *concealed* the structural content that Poincaré and Minkowski had exhibited directly in 1905–1908. The Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster is therefore not just the residue of two traditions developing under different phenomenology; it is the residue of a century of canonical formalism moving *away* from the structural clarity Poincaré and Minkowski had achieved in 1905–1908, with each subsequent development hiding the $+ic$ perpendicularity content one layer deeper inside calculational machinery. The McGucken framework's return to $dx_4/dt = ic$ as the foundational physical principle — with $x_4 = ict$ as its integrated coordinate shadow — is therefore a *return to Poincaré and Minkowski* with the active-expansion content that neither possessed in 1905 or 1908. The McGucken Principle is what Poincaré's and Minkowski's $x_4 = ict$ would have meant if either had recognized it as the integrated shadow of a physical-geometric process — and the relevant historical accident is that Poincaré had the mathematics and explicitly rejected its physical reality, while Minkowski elevated the geometric structure to physical reality but treated it as static rather than dynamical.

This is the historical diagnostic in its full structural form: statistical mechanics evolved in 3D shadow phenomenology and coordinatized the $i$ away; quantum mechanics evolved in $x_4$-direct phenomenology and put the $i$ in by hand; Poincaré 1905/1906 introduced the mathematical structure with $x_4 = ict$ as the imaginary fourth coordinate, then Minkowski 1908 elevated it to a unified geometric interpretation of spacetime as a physical entity; Einstein's signature switch and all subsequent canonical formalism progressively concealed the perpendicularity content; the Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster is the residue of these accumulated historical layers; and the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ is the recognition that all the layers conceal the same underlying physical-geometric content. *The $i$ that statistical mechanics did not need and quantum mechanics could not avoid is the same $i$ — and it is the perpendicularity-factor of the fourth dimension's active expansion at velocity $c$.*


### The Pre-Wick Genealogy of $t \to -i\tau$: From Poincaré 1905 Through Schrödinger 1931 to Wick 1954


The previous subsection identifies Poincaré 1905/1906 and Minkowski 1908 as the historical moments at which the $+ic$ perpendicularity content of $dx_4/dt = ic$ first appeared in canonical literature, with Poincaré supplying the mathematical structure and Minkowski supplying the geometric and ontological interpretation, and Wick 1954 as the moment at which the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ was formalized as a calculational tool in relativistic bound-state physics. The standard contemporary narrative — exemplified by the 2026 Wikipedia article [439] and circulating widely in physics pedagogy — telescopes this history, attributing the "first implicit use" of the Wick rotation to Schwinger and Feynman in the late 1940s. The narrative is historically wrong by approximately forty-four years. The Wick rotation as a coordinate substitution was first used by Henri Poincaré in 1905, three years before Minkowski; it was used as an explicit connector between quantum wave evolution and Markovian diffusion by Erwin Schrödinger in 1931, eighteen years before any Schwinger or Feynman use; and it was formalized in finite-temperature field theory by Takeo Matsubara in 1955, one year *after* Wick. The correction of the historical record is structurally important because the genealogy of $t \to -i\tau$ traces a chain of near-misses spanning fifty years between 1905 and 1955, every one of which is a $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel observation made without the active-expansion content of $dx_4/dt = ic$. We trace the chain in order, with primary sources.

**Poincaré 1905 — the first introduction of $ict$ as a fourth coordinate.** Henri Poincaré's June 5, 1905 *Comptes Rendus* note "Sur la dynamique de l'électron" [394], expanded into the bulky December 1905 / 1906 *Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo* memoir of the same title [395], is the historically first introduction of $ict$ as the fourth coordinate of a relativistic four-dimensional space. Poincaré observed that the Lorentz transformations leave the quadratic form $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2t^2$ invariant, and explicitly noted that they could be regarded as rotations in a four-dimensional space with coordinates $(x, y, z, ict)$. Damour's modern historical reading [402] confirms the priority: Poincaré's 1905 note presents the four-dimensional formalism three years before Minkowski's 1908 Cologne address. The June 1905 publication date predates Einstein's June 30, 1905 *Annalen der Physik* paper "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper" by approximately three weeks. Poincaré's 1905/1906 formulation is therefore the historical origin of the imaginary-time substitution $t \to ict/c = it$ that the contemporary Wick-rotation literature attributes to the late 1940s. The substitution Poincaré used in 1905 is identically the substitution the orthodox literature calls the Wick rotation; the only difference is that Poincaré used it as a relativistic-electrodynamics coordinate identification, not as a calculational device for analytic continuation of quantum amplitudes.

**Minkowski 1908 — the geometric and ontological interpretation, not the four-dimensional formalism itself.** Minkowski's September 21, 1908 Cologne address "Raum und Zeit" [333], published in 1909 in *Physikalische Zeitschrift*, is conventionally credited with the introduction of four-dimensional spacetime. The conventional credit is inaccurate at the level of primary sources. The four-dimensional formalism with imaginary fourth coordinate $ict$, the Lorentz transformations as rotations in that four-dimensional space, the invariant quadratic form $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2 t^2$, the Poincaré group of transformations (formally treated as a group, before Minkowski), the first four-vectors (including a four-current and a four-force), and even the first analysis of gravitation propagating at $c$ with corresponding gravitational waves — all are present already in Poincaré's 1905/1906 *Comptes Rendus* note and *Rendiconti* memoir [394, 395], three years before Minkowski's Cologne lecture. The modern historical analysis by Damour [403] and the comprehensive primary-source study by Walter [404] establish that Minkowski's mathematical formalism contains essentially no new content beyond Poincaré's 1905/1906 results at the level of the four-dimensional coordinate-and-transformation machinery itself.

What Minkowski added is a layer of geometric and ontological interpretation built on top of Poincaré's already-existing mathematical formalism. Six items of genuine addition are identifiable in the primary sources. (1) The phrase and concept of *spacetime* (*Raum-Zeit*) as a single physical entity rather than a mathematical four-dimensional space: the Cologne lecture's famous opening declaration that *"henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality"* is an ontological claim about physical reality, not a mathematical observation. Poincaré had the four-dimensional mathematical structure but explicitly did not believe it carried physical reality; Damour [403] documents that *"although the first discovery of the mathematical structure of the space-time of special relativity is due to Poincaré's great article of July 1905, Poincaré (in contrast to Minkowski) had never believed that this structure could really"* be physically substantive. (2) The *spacetime diagram* — the visual representation with worldlines, light cones, past and future hypercones, simultaneity hyperplanes — is genuinely Minkowski's introduction; Walter [404] establishes that Minkowski's Figure 1 from the Cologne lecture is new and that Poincaré had no such diagrams. (3) The concept of the *worldline* (*Weltlinie*) as the fundamental physical object — a particle's history is its worldline, not a sequence of (position, time) pairs — is Minkowski's. (4) *Proper time* $\tau$ as the invariant parameter along a worldline, enabling correct four-velocity and four-acceleration definitions, is Minkowski's. Walter notes that Minkowski's first attempt at four-velocity in his 1907 colloquium was actually wrong; he corrected it for the 1908 *Grundgleichungen* paper using proper time. (5) The *light cone as a global causal structure* — the recognition that the locus $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2 t^2 = 0$ partitions spacetime into causally distinct timelike-past, timelike-future, and spacelike-elsewhere regions — is Minkowski's. (6) The *full four-tensor calculus for electrodynamics*, with the electromagnetic field tensor $F_{\mu\nu}$ and its dual emerging cleanly from the four-dimensional formalism, is developed in Minkowski's April 1908 *Grundgleichungen* paper to a depth Poincaré had not reached.

The six items are interpretively decisive but mathematically modest extensions of Poincaré's 1905/1906 content. Minkowski himself did not cite Poincaré in the Cologne lecture; Damour [403] identifies this omission as a structural failure of the lecture, and Born subsequently reported that Minkowski had told him the 1905 Einstein paper *"came to him as a great shock"* because Minkowski had reached the same conclusions independently but had not published, *"because he wished first to work out the mathematical structure in all its splendour."* Minkowski never made a priority claim against Einstein or Poincaré; the historical record positions Minkowski as the figure who supplied the geometric and ontological interpretation while Poincaré had supplied the mathematical formalism.

The structural reading for the McGucken framework is sharper than the conventional credit allows. The $+ic$ perpendicularity content that the present paper identifies as load-bearing appears in *Poincaré's 1905/1906 formulation*, not in Minkowski's 1908 reading; the mathematical content of $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) as the imaginary fourth coordinate of a Lorentz-invariant four-dimensional space is Poincaré's, three years before Minkowski. Minkowski's six interpretive additions — spacetime as physical entity, worldlines, spacetime diagrams, proper time, light cones, four-tensor electrodynamics — are themselves consequential, and they made the four-dimensional formalism intelligible to the physics community in a way that Poincaré's purely mathematical presentation had not. But the imaginary-time content itself — the substitution $t \to ict/c = it$ that becomes the Wick rotation forty-six years later — is in the historical record from June 5, 1905, three years before Minkowski's Cologne lecture. The McGucken framework's recognition that $x_4 = ict$ is the integrated coordinate shadow of an active physical-geometric process $dx_4/dt = ic$ is therefore an extension of *Poincaré's* 1905/1906 mathematical structure with the active-expansion content that neither Poincaré nor Minkowski possessed. Poincaré had the mathematics and rejected the physical interpretation; Minkowski had the geometric interpretation and rejected the dynamical content; the McGucken framework supplies the dynamical content as the foundational physical principle, recovering both the mathematical structure (Poincaré 1905/1906) and the geometric interpretation (Minkowski 1908) as theorem-shadows of $dx_4/dt = ic$.

**Sommerfeld 1909 — further development.** Arnold Sommerfeld's 1909 work [396] further developed Minkowski's four-dimensional formalism, specifically applying the $ict$ method to the addition of velocity vectors in special relativity. Sommerfeld's work made the four-dimensional formalism a working tool of relativistic physics, with $ict$ as the fourth coordinate used routinely throughout the 1910s and 1920s. The Born–Pauli school used $ict$ as standard notation; Pauli's 1921 *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften* article on relativity theory [397] systematically uses $X = (x, y, z, ict)$ as the standard four-position vector. The $ict$ formulation was the dominant convention in special relativity for approximately twenty years, from Poincaré 1905 through Einstein's gradual transition to the real-coordinate $(-,+,+,+)$ metric tensor formulation during the development of general relativity 1913–1916.

**Schrödinger 1931 — the first explicit $t \to -i\tau$ connector between quantum mechanics and diffusion.** Erwin Schrödinger's 1931 paper "Über die Umkehrung der Naturgesetze" [248], delivered to the Prussian Academy of Sciences and published in the *Sitzungsberichte*, is the earliest extant explicit use of the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ as a connector between quantum wave evolution (Schrödinger's own 1926 wave equation) and Markovian diffusion (the Smoluchowski–Fokker–Planck heat equation). Schrödinger recognized — five years after publishing the wave equation — that his equation with the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ becomes a diffusion equation, structurally identical to the heat equation of statistical physics. The 1931 paper poses what is now called the *Schrödinger bridge problem*: the question of how to construct a stochastic process whose marginal distributions match given initial and final probability distributions, via the analytic continuation of quantum wave evolution. The modern review by Chetrite, Muratore-Ginanneschi, and Schwieger [251] establishes Schrödinger 1931 as the foundational paper of what is now called the Schrödinger-bridge program in stochastic optimal transport [250]. The substitution $t \to -i\tau$ Schrödinger used in 1931 is identically the substitution Wick used in 1954 and is identically the substitution the contemporary literature calls the Wick rotation.

Schrödinger 1931 is the closest pre-McGucken near-miss in the historical record. Schrödinger had the wave equation; he had the diffusion equation; he had the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ that connects them; he had explicitly noted that the two equations are related by this substitution. What he did not have was the recognition that $\tau = x_4/c$ is a coordinate identity on a real four-dimensional manifold whose fourth axis is physically expanding at $+ic$. Schrödinger treated the substitution as a *formal* connector — a mathematical relation between two equations — rather than as a coordinate-geometric identity with physical content. The Cascade of Near-Misses subsection of the present paper (treating Schrödinger 1926–1944 as the founder's two near-misses) is the structural diagnosis of this gap: Schrödinger came closer than any other pre-McGucken figure to the recognition, and his failure to close the gap is the precise diagnostic of why the orthodox formalism has been unable to supply the physical content from inside.

**Kac 1949 — the Feynman–Kac rigorous formulation.** Mark Kac's 1949 paper "On distributions of certain Wiener functionals" [258] is the rigorous mathematical formulation of what Schrödinger had observed informally in 1931: the matrix elements of the heat-kernel operator $e^{-t\hat H}$ acting on the Schrödinger Hamiltonian $\hat H = -\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + V$ admit a path-integral representation in terms of Wiener-process expectations. Kac was directly motivated by Feynman's 1948 paper "Space-time approach to non-relativistic quantum mechanics" [252], which had introduced the Lorentzian path integral $\int \mathcal{D}\gamma \exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$. Kac recognized that under the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ Feynman's formal path-integral expression becomes the rigorously-defined Wiener-process expectation $\int \mathcal{D}\omega \exp(-S_E[\omega]/\hbar)$, with the Brownian motion measure of Wiener 1923 [398] supplying the rigorous mathematical content that Feynman's formal expression lacked. The Feynman–Kac formula is now standard mathematical physics; its 1949 publication establishes that the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ — fourteen years before Schrödinger 1931 and forty-four years after Poincaré 1905 — was a working tool of mathematical physics in 1949, well before the Schwinger 1958 and Wick 1954 papers that the contemporary narrative attributes the rotation to.

**Wick 1954 — the Bethe-Salpeter formalization.** Gian-Carlo Wick's 1954 *Physical Review* paper "Properties of Bethe-Salpeter Wave Functions" [425] is the paper that gave the rotation its name. Wick's specific application was *not* the connection between quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics — the application that the contemporary literature most often associates with the Wick rotation. Wick's application was the *relativistic two-body bound-state problem* in quantum electrodynamics: the Bethe-Salpeter equation [399] for hydrogen-like bound states with relativistic kinematics. Wick observed that the integration contour in the energy plane could be rotated by 90 degrees from the real axis to the imaginary axis, converting the Minkowski-signature Bethe-Salpeter equation into a Euclidean-signature integral equation that was tractable by standard techniques. The Wick 1954 paper is therefore a *technical* paper on relativistic bound states, not a *conceptual* paper on the QM–statistical-mechanics correspondence. The name "Wick rotation" attached to the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ across all of its uses retrospectively, by analogy with Wick's energy-contour rotation in the Bethe-Salpeter integral.

The historically accurate statement is therefore: Wick 1954 introduced the *name* and the *Bethe-Salpeter application*; the *substitution* itself had been used continuously since Poincaré 1905, with substantive intermediate applications by Schrödinger 1931 (quantum-to-diffusion) and Kac 1949 (Feynman path integral to Wiener integral). The contemporary literature's attribution of the "first implicit use" to Schwinger and Feynman in the late 1940s is wrong by approximately forty years if Poincaré 1905 is the starting point, and approximately twenty years if Schrödinger 1931 is taken as the starting point.

**Matsubara 1955 and Schwinger 1958 — the finite-temperature formalization.** The application of the rotation specifically to the finite-temperature field theory — the application that the Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster identifies as the structural mystery — was developed by Takeo Matsubara in 1955 [255] (the Matsubara-frequency formalism for finite-temperature quantum statistical mechanics) and by Julian Schwinger in 1958 [400] (the "On the Euclidean Structure of Relativistic Field Theory" paper that introduces the Schwinger functions as analytic continuations of Wightman functions). These are the papers in which the operator-correspondence $e^{-i\hat H t/\hbar} \leftrightarrow e^{-\beta \hat H}$ at the heart of the Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster first appears in its modern form. Matsubara is one year after Wick; Schwinger is four years after Wick. Both Matsubara and Schwinger built on Wick's contour-rotation observation, applying it to the finite-temperature regime that Wick himself had not addressed.

**Symanzik 1969 and Osterwalder–Schrader 1973/1975 — the rigorous axiomatization.** Kurt Symanzik's 1969 work on Euclidean field theory [401], followed by Konrad Osterwalder and Robert Schrader's 1973 [426] and 1975 [427] reconstruction theorems, supplied the rigorous mathematical axiomatization of Euclidean quantum field theory and its analytic continuation back to Minkowski space. Osterwalder–Schrader established the reflection-positivity condition under which the analytic continuation is rigorously valid; the reconstruction theorem of Osterwalder–Schrader 1975 establishes that a Euclidean field theory satisfying the OS axioms reconstructs a unique Wightman quantum field theory in Minkowski space. The OS axioms are the modern standard mathematical justification for the Wick rotation as a calculational tool; they are formal-mathematical the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel content without physical-geometric the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel content. The McGucken-Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ (Theorem 6 of [19]) is the Geometric Channel content that complements the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel OS axiomatization (Theorem 6.1 of [3], the Signature-Bridging Theorem).

**The genealogy table.** The complete pre-McGucken genealogy of the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ is:

- 1905 — Poincaré introduces $ict$ as fourth coordinate in *"Sur la dynamique de l'électron"* (relativistic electrodynamics) [394, 395]
- 1908 — Minkowski extends Poincaré's formal observation to four-dimensional geometric formalism with $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) (special relativity, geometric interpretation) [333]
- 1909 — Sommerfeld further develops the $ict$ method for relativistic velocity-vector addition [396]
- 1921 — Pauli's *Encyklopädie* article uses $X = (x, y, z, ict)$ as standard notation [397]
- 1923 — Wiener constructs the rigorous Brownian-motion measure on path space [398]
- 1931 — Schrödinger explicitly uses $t \to -i\tau$ to connect quantum wave evolution and Markovian diffusion [248]
- 1948 — Feynman publishes the Lorentzian path integral $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ [252]
- 1949 — Kac formalizes the Feynman–Kac formula connecting Feynman path integrals to Wiener integrals via $t \to -i\tau$ [258]
- 1953 — Feynman applies Wick-rotated Euclidean techniques to the polaron problem [253]
- 1954 — Wick formalizes the energy-contour rotation in the Bethe-Salpeter equation; the substitution gets his name [425]
- 1955 — Matsubara introduces the imaginary-time formalism for finite-temperature quantum statistical mechanics [255]
- 1957 — Kubo formula for linear response, beginning of the KMS-condition story [256]
- 1958 — Schwinger introduces Euclidean field theory in *"On the Euclidean Structure of Relativistic Field Theory"* [400]
- 1959 — Martin and Schwinger introduce the KMS condition for thermal field theory [257]
- 1965 — Feynman and Hibbs publish *Quantum Mechanics and Path Integrals* with the "amusing result" passage on statistical mechanics from path integrals [254]
- 1969 — Symanzik develops the rigorous Euclidean field theory program [401]
- 1973 — Osterwalder and Schrader publish the reconstruction axioms for Euclidean Green's functions [426]

The genealogy is fifty years long from Poincaré 1905 to Matsubara 1955 (the canonical operator-correspondence application), and seventy years long from Poincaré 1905 to Osterwalder–Schrader 1975 (the canonical rigorous axiomatization).
