## Theorem 22.3: Gravity Equals the Born Rule — the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Reading of the Shared $x_4$-Mode Count on the McGucken Sphere, Closing the Triangle That Standard Entropic-Gravity and Standard Born-From-Entropy Programs Leave Open

### 22.3.1 Statement of the theorem

Under the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ — the fourth dimension physically expanding at rate $c$ from every spacetime event — gravity and the Born rule are the same fact about the expanding McGucken Sphere, read at two scales. Both descend from the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant Haar measure $\mu_H$ on the Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ at every event $p \in \mathcal{M}_G$. Their shared entropy $S = k_B \ln \Omega$ is the count $\Omega$ of $x_4$-advance modes on the Sphere: read as the surface-integrated count on the horizon 2-surface at Schwarzschild radius $r_s$, it is the Bekenstein–Hawking area law and the entropic-gravity mechanism (Verlinde, Jacobson, Padmanabhan, Bianconi); read as the invariant measure on the event Sphere pulled back to Hilbert space, it is the Born rule. The chain is:

$$\text{gravity} \;\;\longleftrightarrow\;\; k_B \ln \Omega \big|_{\text{horizon}} \;\;=\;\; k_B \ln \Omega \big|_{\text{event}} \;\;\longleftrightarrow\;\; \text{Born rule}$$

with the equality in the middle a theorem of the Haar-measure uniqueness on $\Sigma_+(p)$ (Theorem 7 of this paper) and the fact that horizon and event readings differ only in the scale over which the measure is integrated.

### 22.3.2 The literature landscape — three lines that stop short of closing the triangle

**Line A: gravity = entropy.** Jacobson [122] derived the Einstein field equations from the first law $\delta Q = T\delta S$ applied to local Rindler horizons, with $S = A/(4\ell_P^2)$ as the Bekenstein–Hawking horizon entropy. Verlinde [156] proposed gravity as an entropic force from holographic screens with entropy $S(A) = A/(4\ell_P^2)$ playing the role of Newton's constant's origin. Padmanabhan [470] extended the derivation to cosmic-space expansion via the surface-vs-bulk degree-of-freedom mismatch $dV/dt = \ell_P^2(N_{\text{sur}} - N_{\text{bulk}})$. Bianconi [476] (Phys. Rev. D 111:066001, 2025) built the gravitational action as the quantum relative entropy $D_{\text{rel}}(g\|G) = \mathrm{Tr}[g \ln g - g \ln G]$ between the spacetime metric $g$ and a matter-induced metric $G$, with the Einstein–Hilbert action recovered in the low-coupling limit. Every paper in Line A uses a horizon-scale or metric-scale entropy; none derives the Born rule from its entropy.

**Line B: Born rule = entropy.** Wootters [477] (Phys. Rev. D 23:357, 1981) established that the Fubini–Study metric on projective Hilbert space equals the Fisher–Rao statistical distance derived from measurement outcomes — the Born rule as the unique map that identifies the state-space geometry with the statistical geometry. Braunstein and Caves [478] (Phys. Rev. Lett. 72:3439, 1994) generalised the identification to arbitrary POVMs. Brody and Hughston [479] developed the geometric-quantum-mechanics reading of Born as an invariant measure on projective Hilbert space. Zurek [487] (Phys. Rev. Lett. 90:120404, 2003; Phys. Rev. A 71:052105, 2005) derived the Born rule from entanglement-assisted invariance (envariance) — a symmetry-and-measure route in which the Born weights $p = |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2$ follow uniquely from the invariance properties of composite entangled states. Fivel [488] (arXiv:1010.5300, Found. Phys. 42:291, 2012) derived quantum mechanics including the Born rule from five information-theoretic axioms, with Axiom IV naming the entropy-reduction phenomenon in measurement. Ojima, Okamura, and Saigo [489] (arXiv:1304.6618) derived the Born rule on von Neumann algebras via spectral equivalence, generalising Ozawa's perfect-correlation concept. Chiribella, D'Ariano, and Perinotti [490] (Phys. Rev. A 84:012311, 2011) derived quantum theory from six operational axioms with the Born rule emerging as a consequence. Carcassi and Aidala [480] (Assumptions of Physics essay, June 15, 2026) established that defining the Born rule over pure states is equivalent to defining the von Neumann entropy over an equal mixture $\rho = \tfrac{1}{2}\psi + \tfrac{1}{2}\phi$: the entropy $S(\rho)$ is an invertible function of the conditional probability $p(\psi|\phi)$, so specifying either determines the other. [481] (Entropy 27:898, 2025) derived the Born rule as the unique minimizer of Umegaki relative entropy across measurement contexts — Petz's Pythagorean identity making dephasing the minimum-entropy projection; the Born weights $p_C(i) = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho P_i)$ arise as a variational consequence rather than an axiom. [482] (arXiv:0909.4995) supplied a geometric interpretation of Shannon entropy from the Born rule. [483] (arXiv:2603.11900) placed the Born rule inside a broader "existence as distinguishability" programme. Every paper in Line B uses a state-space or information-geometric entropy; none derives gravity from its entropy.

**Line C: attempted bridges.** Munkhammar [484] (arXiv:1003.1262, 2010) proposed that Verlinde's entropic gravity has a quantum-mechanical origin, feeding the Born probability density $|\psi|^2$ into the holographic entropy that sources the gravitational law. This is the closest published attempt to place the Born density on the gravity side. Munkhammar does not derive gravity from the Born rule; he uses the Born density as an input to entropic gravity, and lists both a relativistic extension and the derivation of the identification itself as open problems. Lee [485] (arXiv:1003.4464) connected entropic gravity to quantum information loss at horizons — gravity from quantum information, but not from the Born rule specifically. Süzen [491] (arXiv:1612.00288) proposed a testable link between Verlinde's entropic gravity and the Diósi–Penrose gravity-induced wavefunction collapse mechanism, offering a matter-wave interferometry protocol to distinguish the entropic-gravity + Diósi–Penrose scheme from standard quantum mechanics. Valentini [486] (Found. Phys. 53:6, 2023; arXiv:2212.12175) argued the opposite direction: at the fundamental quantum-gravity scale (non-normalizable Wheeler–DeWitt wave functional $\Psi$) there is no Born rule; the Born rule emerges only in the semiclassical regime with normalisable Schrödinger wave functions on a classical spacetime background. Valentini's programme stands as the direct counter-position to the identification argued for in this section; the two frameworks make distinguishable predictions for quantum-gravity-regime experiments, and the McGucken reading answers Valentini directly in §22.3.6 below.

**The open triangle.** The literature has $\text{gravity} = \text{entropy}$ (Line A). The literature has $\text{Born rule} = \text{entropy}$ (Line B). The transitive step $\text{gravity} = \text{Born rule}$ has not been made. The gap is not accidental. It follows from the fact that Line A's entropy (horizon area count, or metric relative entropy) and Line B's entropy (state-space information geometry, or von Neumann entropy) are different mathematical objects with different domains. Without a physical mechanism identifying the two, the transitive step cannot run.

### 22.3.3 The McGucken derivation — one entropy, two readings

The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies the physical mechanism that identifies Line A's entropy and Line B's entropy as the same physical object at two different scales of integration.

**Step 1: the Sphere at every event.** By the Principle, the fourth dimension expands at rate $c$ in a spherically symmetric manner from every event $p \in \mathcal{M}_G$. The geometric realisation of this expansion at $p$ is the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ — the wavefront of radius $ct$ around $p$ swept out by the $x_4$-expansion. The Sphere is present at every event of $\mathcal{M}_G$ without exception (Theorem 3 of the present paper).

**Step 2: the Haar measure as the unique invariant on the Sphere.** By $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetry of the Sphere and the Haar–von Neumann uniqueness theorem, there is a unique bi-invariant probability measure $\mu_H$ on $\Sigma_+(p)$ (Theorem 7 of the present paper). This measure is derived from the physical geometry of the expansion at $p$; it replaces Gibbs's postulate of equal *a priori* probabilities [227] with a theorem.

**Step 3: the state count $\Omega$.** Let $\Omega$ denote the number of $x_4$-advance modes distinguishable on $\Sigma_+(p)$ at the working resolution (Planck-scale for horizon-tier applications, arbitrary spatial-detector resolution for event-tier applications). $\Omega$ is the count that the Haar measure $\mu_H$ normalizes over. The Boltzmann entropy of the Sphere at resolution scale is $S = k_B \ln \Omega$ — a physical count of the $x_4$-advance modes the Sphere supports at that scale.

**Step 4: the horizon reading — gravity.** For a Schwarzschild black hole of horizon radius $r_s$, the horizon 2-surface is a specific McGucken Sphere at fixed radius. The Planck-scale $x_4$-mode count on this Sphere is $\Omega_{\text{horizon}} = A/\ell_P^2$ where $A = 4\pi r_s^2$; the entropy is $S_{BH} = k_B \ln \Omega_{\text{horizon}} = k_B A/(4\ell_P^2)$ up to the standard normalization (Theorem 15 of the present paper, replacing the Bekenstein 1973 postulate and the Hawking 1975 semi-classical derivation with the McGucken-Sphere direct derivation). The Hawking temperature $T_H = \hbar/(k_B \beta_H) = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$ arises from the Euclidean-cigar closure of the $x_4$-axis at circumference $L_H = 4\pi r_s$ (Theorem 16 of the present paper, and Chapter 15bis of [McWick]). The Einstein field equations follow from the first law $\delta Q = T_H \delta S$ applied to the horizon, via the Jacobson route (Theorem 19.4 of the present paper, the Hilbert–Jacobson Agreement). This is the McGucken-Sphere derivation of the Line A result: gravity as horizon thermodynamics of the Sphere.

**Step 5: the event reading — Born rule.** At the event scale, the same Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ carries the same Haar measure $\mu_H$. Pulled back to Hilbert space via the Sphere-to-Hilbert-space cogeneration ([61], [25]), $\mu_H$ becomes the Born-rule probability measure on rays: $p(\psi|\phi) = |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2/(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\phi\rangle)$. The specific quadratic form of the Born rule is the Haar-measure inner product on rays; the squaring is the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariance requirement on the measure. This is the McGucken-Sphere derivation of the Line B result: Born rule as the invariant measure of the Sphere.

**Step 6: the identification.** The count $\Omega$ in Step 3 is the same physical object in Steps 4 and 5. At the horizon scale, $\Omega = A/\ell_P^2$ is the tally of Planck-scale Spheres tiling the horizon 2-surface; the entropy is $S_{BH}$. At the event scale, $\Omega$ is the tally of Haar-measure-weighted $x_4$-outcomes the Sphere supports at detector resolution; the entropy is the Shannon entropy of the Born distribution on the Sphere, which by Carcassi–Aidala's equivalence [480] equals the von Neumann entropy of the corresponding density matrix. The two entropies are the same physical count of $x_4$-modes on the same Sphere, read at two different scales of integration. This identity is what the standard literature does not have and cannot produce, because the standard literature has no physical mechanism generating both the horizon entropy and the state-space entropy from a shared object.

### 22.3.4 The transitive equivalence

Combining Steps 4, 5, and 6:

$$\text{gravity} \;\;\stackrel{\text{Steps 4, T15, T19.4}}{\longleftrightarrow}\;\; S_{\text{horizon}} = k_B \ln \Omega \;\;\stackrel{\text{Step 6, T7 uniqueness}}{=}\;\; k_B \ln \Omega \;\;\stackrel{\text{Steps 5, T7 pullback}}{\longleftrightarrow}\;\; \text{Born rule}$$

Each of the three arrows is a derived theorem of the McGucken Principle:
- The first arrow is Theorem 15 (Bekenstein–Hawking as Planck-sphere tiling) combined with Theorem 19.4 (Hilbert–Jacobson Agreement), giving the Einstein equations from horizon thermodynamics.
- The middle equality is Theorem 7 (Haar-measure uniqueness on the Sphere): the same $\mu_H$ counts states at both scales.
- The third arrow is the Sphere-to-Hilbert-space cogeneration [61], giving the Born rule as the pullback of $\mu_H$ to rays.

The chain closes because the entropy in the middle is one physical object (the count of $x_4$-modes on the Sphere generated by $dx_4/dt = ic$), not two coincidentally-named objects.

### 22.3.5 The identification lives at the Sphere-level, before the channel decomposition

Theorem 19 of the present paper (the McGucken Duality) established that $dx_4/dt = ic$ generates physics through two channels: a Geometric Channel (Lagrangian route, spatial-three-slice geometry, Einstein–Hilbert action, Ricci curvature) and an Algebraic Channel (Hamiltonian route, non-commutative operator algebra, canonical commutator $[\hat q, \hat p] = i\hbar$, Hilbert space). The tempting reading — Geometric Channel gives gravity, Algebraic Channel gives Born rule — misplaces where the identification sits. Both quantities are derivable via either channel, and it is precisely this that makes gravity $=$ Born rule a Sphere-level fact rather than a cross-channel coincidence.

**The four corners of the derivation matrix.** All four routes exist in the McGucken corpus and in the wider literature the McGucken framework subsumes:

- **Gravity via the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel.** Sphere at every event $\to$ null hypersurface $\to$ Jacobson's first law $\delta Q = T \delta S$ applied to the horizon $\to$ Einstein field equations. This is the Hilbert–Jacobson Agreement of Theorem 19.4, corresponding to the Verlinde [156], Jacobson [122], Padmanabhan [470] line externally.
- **Gravity via the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel.** Sphere-generated operator algebra $\to$ metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ read as a quantum operator on the Sphere's Hilbert space $\to$ quantum relative entropy $D_{\text{rel}}(g \| G)$ between $g$ and a matter-induced operator $G$ as the gravitational action $\to$ Einstein–Hilbert action in the low-coupling limit. This is Bianconi's [476] approach, and it lives on the Algebraic Channel side of the Duality.
- **Born rule vian Algebraic Channel.** Sphere at every event $\to$ $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant Haar measure $\to$ pullback to Hilbert-space rays via the cogeneration of [61], [25] $\to$ $p(\psi|\phi) = |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2$. This is the standard route and corresponds to Zurek's envariance programme externally.
- **Born rule via Geometric Channel.** Sphere at every event $\to$ Fubini–Study metric on the space of rays $\to$ Wootters's [477] identification of the Fubini–Study metric with the Fisher–Rao statistical distance derived from measurement outcomes $\to$ Born rule as the unique map making state-space geometry and statistical geometry coincide. Braunstein–Caves [478] generalise to POVMs; Brody–Hughston [479] develop the geometric-quantum-mechanics formulation. This is a purely Geometric-Channel derivation of the Born rule.

**Why the four-corner completeness matters.** If the Geometric Channel gave only gravity and the Algebraic Channel gave only Born rule, then their equality $\text{gravity} = \text{Born rule}$ would be a cross-channel bridge — one physical fact accessible through two mathematical routes that meet by external construction. The four-corner completeness shows that the equality lives one level deeper: gravity and the Born rule are both facts about the shared Sphere and its Haar measure, and every channel that can access the Sphere sees both facts. The Geometric Channel derives both quantities (gravity via null-hypersurface thermodynamics, Born rule via Fubini–Study $=$ Fisher–Rao); the Algebraic Channel derives both quantities (gravity via operator-metric quantum relative entropy, Born rule via ray-space pullback). The identification is a Sphere-level identity that both channels report from their respective vantage points.

**Where the Planck-length scale bridge enters.** Theorem 19.5.2 (the Bi-Resolution Diagnostic) supplies the scale identification that makes the Sphere's mode count $\Omega$ well-defined at both the horizon scale and the event scale: the Planck length $\ell_P$ is the Lorentz-scalar discreteness bridge. At the horizon scale, $\Omega = A/\ell_P^2$ is the Planck-sphere tiling count; at the event scale, $\Omega$ is the number of Haar-measure-weighted $x_4$-outcomes at the detector's resolution. Both scales use the same $\ell_P$-normalised $\mu_H$; the two counts differ only by the domain of integration.

**Summary.** The identification $\text{gravity} = \text{Born rule}$ is a Sphere-level identity that both channels of the McGucken Duality independently confirm. The Geometric Channel confirms it by deriving both quantities from Sphere-geometry (null hypersurface for gravity, Fubini–Study for Born rule); the Algebraic Channel confirms it by deriving both quantities from Sphere-generated operator algebra (metric as quantum operator for gravity, ray-space Haar measure for Born rule). The identification holds prior to the channel decomposition: the fact stands regardless of which channel is used to compute either quantity, and it is precisely this channel-independence that places the equality at the Sphere level rather than at the level of a cross-channel bridge.

### 22.3.6 What the literature does not have and why; and the direct response to Valentini's counter-position

Line A's entropy is a count of horizon-area cells in units of $\ell_P^2$. Line B's entropy is a count of Hilbert-space dimensions weighted by von Neumann probabilities. Without a physical object at both scales carrying a single measure, the two entropies cannot be identified. Jacobson's derivation of the Einstein equations uses the Bekenstein–Hawking area law as an input; the area law's physical origin (why $S = A/(4\ell_P^2)$ and not $S = \alpha A^{1/2}$ for some other exponent) is not derived in Jacobson's programme. Verlinde's entropic gravity uses the equipartition theorem on holographic screens; the screens' physical status and the equipartition assumption are inputs. Bianconi's quantum-relative-entropy action uses the spacetime metric as a density-matrix-like operator; the physical origin of this identification is left as a mathematical assumption. Carcassi–Aidala's Born-rule / von Neumann-entropy equivalence is a formal identity on the abstract state space; the physical origin of either quantity is not derived. The Contextual Relative-Entropy Minimization derivation [481] uses measurement-context axioms; the physical origin of the contexts is not derived. The information-theoretic derivations of Zurek [487], Fivel [488], Ojima–Okamura–Saigo [489], and Chiribella–D'Ariano–Perinotti [490] all derive the Born rule from axioms on the abstract state space; none supplies a physical mechanism generating the state space itself, and none derives gravity from its axioms.

**The sharper statement — same Haar measure, different scale of integration.** The McGucken framework supplies what all of these programmes leave implicit: the Sphere at every event generated by $dx_4/dt = ic$, carrying the unique $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant Haar measure $\mu_H$. This one measure supports two operations:
- **evaluated at the event**, $\mu_H$ pulls back to Hilbert space via the cogeneration of [61], [25] and becomes the Born-rule probability measure on rays: $p(\psi|\phi) = |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2$;
- **integrated over the horizon**, $\mu_H$ tiles the horizon 2-surface with Planck-scale Sphere cells and gives the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy $S_{BH} = k_B A/(4\ell_P^2)$ from which Jacobson's route yields the Einstein field equations.

Same $\mu_H$; different scale of integration. This is the compactest statement of the identification: gravity and the Born rule are two integrals of one physical measure on one physical object (the Sphere at every event), evaluated at two different scales (horizon-integrated versus event-pointwise). The two entropies of Lines A and B, which the standard programmes treat as different mathematical objects, are the same $\mu_H$-supported $x_4$-mode count read at two different scales.

**Direct response to Valentini's counter-position.** Valentini [486] argues from the de Broglie–Bohm pilot-wave formulation of quantum gravity that at the fundamental scale (non-normalizable Wheeler–DeWitt wave functional $\Psi$) there is no Born rule, and that Born-rule statistics emerge only in the semiclassical regime with normalisable Schrödinger wave functions on a classical spacetime background. The McGucken reading answers Valentini directly: in the McGucken framework the Born rule holds wherever $dx_4/dt = ic$ generates a Sphere, and $dx_4/dt = ic$ holds at every event of $\mathcal{M}_G$ (Principle universality). The Born rule therefore holds at every event, including horizon events and events near the classical singularity of a black hole. The regime Valentini identifies as pre-Born (non-normalizable $\Psi$) corresponds in the McGucken framework to a regime where the Wheeler–DeWitt formalism itself becomes inapplicable, not to a regime where the physical Born-rule measure fails; the semiclassical emergence Valentini derives is the emergence of the Wheeler–DeWitt approximation to the physical Sphere-based measure that was already present. The two frameworks make distinguishable predictions: Valentini's programme predicts detectable Born-rule violation for gravitationally-influenced quantum systems in specific relic-cosmological regimes (with primordial power-spectrum signatures at large scales); the McGucken framework predicts that Born-rule tests in all gravitational contexts (including strong-field regimes near horizons, if experimentally accessible) will respect the identification $\text{gravity} = \text{Born rule}$ derived here. The Süzen [491] and Munkhammar [484] proposals for matter-wave-interferometry tests of the gravity–quantum-probability link are the operationally most accessible experimental probes.

### 22.3.7 Falsifiability

Theorem 22.3 is falsifiable in the same sense as the theorems it depends on. Any of the following would refute it:
1. A demonstration that the Haar measure on $\Sigma_+(p)$ does not give the Born rule when pulled back to Hilbert space via the [MGHilbertBorn] cogeneration. This would refute Theorem 7 or the pullback theorem.
2. A demonstration that the horizon entropy $S_{BH}$ has a value different from the Planck-sphere tiling count $A/(4\ell_P^2)$ at leading order. This would refute Theorem 15.
3. A demonstration that the two counts (horizon-tiling count and event-Sphere pullback count) differ by more than a scale factor at any resolution where both are defined. This would refute the identification of Step 6.
4. Empirical detection of Born-rule violation in a regime where gravity plays a role, in a way that cannot be attributed to any of the standard non-Born-rule proposals (Valentini's semiclassical relaxation, Diósi–Penrose collapse, GRW spontaneous localization). Such a detection would show that gravity and Born rule are not the same fact, and would refute Theorem 22.3 directly.

Falsification path (4) is the operationally distinguishing one: no other framework in the current literature makes the gravity–Born identification, so no other framework predicts that Born-rule tests in gravitational contexts must respect the identification. The Munkhammar prediction (arXiv:1003.1262) of a gravitational effect on the quantum wavefunction and the Süzen prediction (arXiv:1612.00288) of a testable link between gravitational constant and quantum-state via matter-wave interferometry are compatible with the McGucken identification and are refinable within it.

### 22.3.8 What Theorem 22.3 adds to the McGucken corpus

Theorem 22.3 closes the theorem chain of the present paper by identifying two of its principal endpoints — the gravity results of Theorems 15–18 and the Born-rule pullback of Theorem 7 — as the same physical fact about the shared McGucken Sphere. The identification is a corollary of Theorem 7 (Haar-measure uniqueness on $\Sigma_+(p)$), Theorem 15 (Bekenstein–Hawking as Planck-sphere tiling), Theorem 19 (the McGucken Duality's two channels), Theorem 19.5.2 (Planck-length scale-bridging), and the Sphere-to-Hilbert-space cogeneration of [61]. It is a derived theorem of the McGucken corpus, not a metaphysical assertion.

The single physical entropy — the count of $x_4$-advance modes on the McGucken Sphere at the working scale — subsumes both the horizon entropy of the Bekenstein–Hawking–Jacobson–Verlinde–Padmanabhan–Bianconi line and the state-space entropy of the Wootters–Braunstein–Caves–Brody–Hughston–Carcassi–Aidala line. Gravity is that entropy read as an integrated count over the horizon 2-surface; the Born rule is that entropy read as an invariant measure at the event, pulled back to Hilbert space. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ is the physical fact that generates both.



### 22.3.9 Araki–Uhlmann relative entropy as a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ — the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ von-Neumann-algebra generalization of the Step-5 Umegaki material, via Tomita–Takesaki standard form on the wedge algebra with modular conjugation $J$ identified as PT reflection through the source event per Bisognano–Wichmann 1975/1976

**McGucken Principle anchor.** Under $dx_4/dt = ic$ the fourth dimension expands at the velocity of light $c$ in a spherically symmetric manner from every spacetime event, with the imaginary unit $i$ marking perpendicularity of $x_4$ to the three spatial axes $x_1, x_2, x_3$ and with the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ at every event $p$ carrying the Compton wavelength $\lambda_C = h/(mc)$ that sets the quantum of action $h = \lambda_C \cdot mc$ per Compton-cycle of its $x_4$-expansion (Theorem 22.5.4 of the present paper, the two-bounds architecture: $\hbar$ as entropy floor, $c$ as speed ceiling, both attributes of the one Sphere). Theorem 22.3's four-corner identification of gravity $=$ Born rule as the same $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant Haar measure $\mu_H$ on $\Sigma_+(p)$ read at two scales of integration (horizon-integrated versus event-pointwise) covers the finite-dimensional (type-$\mathrm{I}_n$) case through the Umegaki 1962 relative entropy $S(\rho \| \sigma) = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho \log \rho - \rho \log \sigma)$ cited at reference [481] (ContextualBornEntropy2025) in Line B of §22.3.2 and at Bianconi 2025 reference [476] in Line A. The present subsection lifts this identification from the type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ setting to the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ von-Neumann-algebra setting that algebraic quantum field theory requires at horizons and wedges, by deriving the Araki 1976/1977 relative entropy of states on the Sphere-cogenerated wedge algebra as a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$, with the Tomita–Takesaki modular conjugation $J$ identified geometrically through the Bisognano–Wichmann 1975/1976 theorem as PT (parity-time) reflection through the source event $p$. The Uhlmann 1977 monotonicity of the Araki relative entropy under completely positive unital normal maps — the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ data-processing inequality that generalizes the Lindblad 1975 monotonicity of the Umegaki relative entropy under completely positive maps on finite-dimensional matrix algebras — is derived in §22.3.10 below from the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Haar-measure contraction under coarse-graining of the McGucken Sphere via the Stinespring 1955 dilation.

**Tomita–Takesaki standard-form notation.** For a von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$ (algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ closed under weak-operator topology and containing the identity) acting on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, the *standard form* (Araki 1974, *Pacific J. Math.* **50**, 309–354; Haagerup 1975, *Math. Scand.* **37**, 271–283) is the quadruple $(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{H}, J, \mathcal{P})$ where:
- $\mathcal{M}$ is the observable algebra;
- $\mathcal{H}$ is the Hilbert space on which $\mathcal{M}$ acts;
- $J : \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{H}$ is an antiunitary involution ($J^2 = \mathbf{1}$, $\langle J\xi | J\eta \rangle = \langle\eta|\xi\rangle$), called the *modular conjugation*;
- $\mathcal{P} \subset \mathcal{H}$ is a closed convex self-dual cone, called the *natural positive cone*;

satisfying: (a) $J \mathcal{M} J = \mathcal{M}'$ where $\mathcal{M}'$ is the commutant of $\mathcal{M}$; (b) $J \xi = \xi$ for all $\xi \in \mathcal{P}$; (c) $a J a J \in \mathcal{P}$ for all $a \in \mathcal{M}$; (d) every normal state $\varphi$ on $\mathcal{M}$ is represented by a unique vector $\Phi \in \mathcal{P}$ with $\varphi(a) = \langle\Phi | a\Phi\rangle$ for all $a \in \mathcal{M}$. The Haagerup 1975 theorem states that the standard form exists and is unique up to unitary equivalence for every von Neumann algebra.

For a cyclic separating vector $\Phi \in \mathcal{H}$ for $\mathcal{M}$ (meaning the subspace $\mathcal{M}\Phi$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$, and $a\Phi = 0$ with $a \in \mathcal{M}$ implies $a = 0$), the *Tomita operator* $S_\Phi$ is the closed antilinear operator defined by $S_\Phi(a\Phi) = a^* \Phi$ for all $a \in \mathcal{M}$. Its polar decomposition
$$S_\Phi = J \Delta_\Phi^{1/2}$$
defines the *modular operator* $\Delta_\Phi$ (positive self-adjoint, generally unbounded) and the modular conjugation $J$. The *Tomita–Takesaki theorem* (Takesaki 1970, *Lecture Notes in Mathematics* **128**, Springer, Berlin) states:
$$\Delta_\Phi^{it} \, \mathcal{M} \, \Delta_\Phi^{-it} = \mathcal{M} \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R},$$
so the *modular flow* $\sigma_t^\varphi(a) \equiv \Delta_\Phi^{it} a \Delta_\Phi^{-it}$ is a one-parameter group of automorphisms of $\mathcal{M}$. The state $\varphi(a) = \langle\Phi | a\Phi\rangle$ is a KMS state with respect to $\sigma_t^\varphi$ at inverse temperature $-1$:
$$\varphi(a \, \sigma_{-i}^\varphi(b)) = \varphi(ba) \quad \text{for } a, b \in \mathcal{M}$$
(KMS condition in the Haag–Hugenholtz–Winnink 1967 formulation, *Commun. Math. Phys.* **5**, 215–236).

**Relative modular operator.** For two faithful normal states $\varphi, \psi$ on $\mathcal{M}$ with representing vectors $\Phi, \Psi \in \mathcal{P}$ (both cyclic separating), the *relative Tomita operator* $S_{\Psi|\Phi}$ is defined (Araki 1973, "Relative Hamiltonian for faithful normal states of a von Neumann algebra," *Publ. RIMS Kyoto Univ.* **9**, 165–209) by closing the map
$$S_{\Psi|\Phi}(a\Phi) = a^* \Psi \quad \text{for } a \in \mathcal{M}.$$
Its polar decomposition
$$S_{\Psi|\Phi} = J \Delta_{\Psi|\Phi}^{1/2}$$
defines the *relative modular operator* $\Delta_{\Psi|\Phi}$. When $\Psi = \Phi$, $\Delta_{\Psi|\Phi}$ reduces to the modular operator $\Delta_\Phi$. The modular conjugation $J$ in the polar decomposition is the same $J$ of the standard form (independent of which state is used).

**Araki relative entropy.** The *Araki relative entropy* of $\varphi$ with respect to $\psi$ (Araki 1976, "Relative entropy of states of von Neumann algebras," *Publ. RIMS Kyoto Univ.* **11** (3), 809–833, Eq. (1-1), p. 809) is
$$\boxed{\; S(\varphi \| \psi) \;=\; \begin{cases} -\langle\Phi \,|\, \log \Delta_{\Psi|\Phi} \,|\, \Phi\rangle, & \text{if } \mathrm{supp}(\varphi) \leq \mathrm{supp}(\psi), \\ +\infty, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\;}$$
Araki 1977 (*Publ. RIMS Kyoto Univ.* **13**, 173–192) proves: (a) non-negativity $S(\varphi\|\psi) \geq 0$ with equality iff $\varphi = \psi$; (b) joint lower semi-continuity in $(\varphi, \psi)$; (c) joint convexity; (d) reduction to the Umegaki form in the type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ case.

**Type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ reduction.** When $\mathcal{M} = B(\mathcal{H})$ with $\dim \mathcal{H} = n < \infty$ (type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ factor), the states $\varphi, \psi$ are represented by density matrices $\rho_\varphi, \rho_\psi$, and the relative modular operator acts on $\mathcal{H} \otimes \overline{\mathcal{H}}$ as the operator $\rho_\psi \otimes \rho_\varphi^{-1}$ (where $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$ is the complex-conjugate Hilbert space and $\mathcal{H} \otimes \overline{\mathcal{H}}$ is the Hilbert–Schmidt representation space). The Araki entropy reduces to the Umegaki 1962 form (Umegaki, "Conditional expectation in an operator algebra, IV (entropy and information)," *Kodai Math. Sem. Rep.* **14**, 59–85):
$$S(\varphi \| \psi) = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_\varphi \log \rho_\varphi - \rho_\varphi \log \rho_\psi),$$
which is the Line-B entropy of Theorem 22.3 Step 5 cited at reference [481] (ContextualBornEntropy2025, *Entropy* **27**(9), 898) and the Line-A entropy cited at reference [476] (Bianconi 2025, *Phys. Rev. D* **111**, 066001). The type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ reduction is what makes Theorem 22.3's four-corner identification applicable in both the horizon-tier Bekenstein–Hawking regime and the event-tier Born-rule regime at finite resolution.

**Theorem 22.3.9 (Araki–Uhlmann relative entropy as a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ — standard-form derivation on the wedge algebra generated by the McGucken Sphere).** *Let $p$ be an event of $\mathcal{M}_G$ with McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ generated at rate $c$ in the $+ic$ direction by $dx_4/dt = ic$. Let $W_R(p)$ be the right Rindler wedge of $p$ — the maximal causal diamond of a uniformly accelerated worldline passing through $p$, specifically the region $\{x : x^1 > |x^0|\}$ with origin translated to $p$. Then:*

*(i) **(Wedge algebra, type-$\mathrm{III}_1$)** The algebra of local observables on $W_R(p)$ is a von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$ of Murray–von Neumann type $\mathrm{III}_1$ (Araki 1964, "Type of von Neumann algebra associated with free field," Prog. Theor. Phys. **32**, 956–965, establishing type $\mathrm{III}$ for the free scalar field; Fredenhagen 1985, "On the modular structure of local algebras of observables," Commun. Math. Phys. **97** (1), 79–89, refining to type $\mathrm{III}_1$ for all local algebras in asymptotically scale-invariant quantum field theories via the asymptotic-scale-invariance argument on the modular-operator spectra; Buchholz–D'Antoni–Fredenhagen 1987, "The universal structure of local algebras," Commun. Math. Phys. **111** (1), 123–135, extending the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ characterization to the universal structure of local algebras), acting on the Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of the Minkowski-space / Hilbert-space cogeneration [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert]. The type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ character is what prevents a direct trace-class density-matrix representation and is why the Umegaki form of Theorem 22.3 Step 5 does not extend directly: a general type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ relative entropy requires the modular-theoretic formulation of Araki 1976.*

*(ii) **(Reeh–Schlieder cyclic separating vacuum)** The vacuum state $\Omega$ is cyclic and separating for $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$ by the Reeh–Schlieder theorem (Reeh and Schlieder 1961, "Bemerkungen zur Unitäräquivalenz von Lorentzinvarianten Feldern," Nuovo Cimento **22**, 1051–1068). Under $dx_4/dt = ic$, the Reeh–Schlieder theorem is a derived consequence of the Principle's universality at every event (Theorem 3 of the present paper) combined with the Wightman-axiom reconstruction of the Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert space [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, §§III-IV]: cyclicity follows from the density of $\mathcal{M}(W_R)\Omega$ in $\mathcal{H}$ (every state is approximable by local operations in any open region), and the separating property follows from locality (the commutant structure of the Haag–Kastler net).*

*(iii) **(Standard form existence and uniqueness)** The standard form $(\mathcal{M}(W_R), \mathcal{H}, J, \mathcal{P})$ exists and is unique up to unitary equivalence (Haagerup 1975, "The standard form of von Neumann algebras," Math. Scand. **37**, 271–283, Theorem 1.6).*

*(iv) **(Bisognano–Wichmann geometric identification of modular objects)** The modular objects for the wedge algebra are identified geometrically by the Bisognano–Wichmann theorem (Bisognano and Wichmann 1975, "On the duality condition for a Hermitian scalar field," J. Math. Phys. **16**, 985–1007, for the Hermitian scalar case; Bisognano and Wichmann 1976, "On the duality condition for quantum fields," J. Math. Phys. **17**, 303–321, for general Wightman fields):*
$$\Delta_\Omega^{it} = U(\Lambda_{x^1}(-2\pi t)), \qquad J = \Theta \cdot R_1(\pi),$$
*where $U$ is the unitary representation of the Poincaré group on $\mathcal{H}$, $\Lambda_{x^1}(s)$ is the Lorentz boost with rapidity $s$ in the $x^1$-direction, $\Theta$ is CPT (charge-parity-time) conjugation (Lüders 1954; Pauli 1955), and $R_1(\pi)$ is the spatial rotation by angle $\pi$ about the $x^1$-axis. For a Hermitian scalar field $\phi(x)$ localized at spacetime point $x = (x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3)$, the modular conjugation acts as*
$$J \,\phi(x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3) \, J^{-1} = \phi^*(-x^0, -x^1, x^2, x^3),$$
*which is a reflection in the $(x^0, x^1)$-plane (fixing $x^2, x^3$) composed with Hermitian conjugation of the field.*

*(v) **(McGucken reading of $J$ as PT reflection through the source event $p$)** Under the McGucken-Wick coordinate identification $\tau_W = x_4/c$ ([McWick, Theorem 30.9.2]) and the Minkowski-space coordinate relation $x_4 = ict$, the $x^0$-reflection $x^0 \mapsto -x^0$ of (iv) corresponds to the $x_4$-reflection $x_4 \mapsto -x_4$. This is the geometric operation that would swap the forward McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ and the time-reversed Sphere $\Sigma_-(p)$. Under $dx_4/dt = +ic$ (sign fixed by Theorem 3 property (c) of the present paper as a physical fact of the Principle), the backward Sphere $\Sigma_-(p)$ is geometrically excluded; the modular conjugation $J$ therefore acts at the single-Sphere level as the formal PT reflection through $p$ — the operation that, if executed on the realized Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$, would produce the excluded $\Sigma_-(p)$. This PT identification supplies the geometry that the orthodox Bisognano–Wichmann treatment leaves at the level of formal CPT conjugation + spatial rotation.*

*(vi) **(Modular flow as Wick-rotated $x_4$-translation and KMS/Unruh identification)** The modular flow $\sigma_t^\Omega(a) = \Delta_\Omega^{it} a \Delta_\Omega^{-it}$ is the Lorentz boost in the $(x^0, x^1)$-direction with boost parameter $-2\pi t$. Under the McGucken-Wick identification $\tau_W = x_4/c$, this boost is the Wick-rotated $x_4$-translation generator — the Euclidean rotation in the $(\tau_W, x^1)$-plane by angle $2\pi t$, closing on itself at $t = 1$ (period one, i.e., KMS periodicity $\tau_W = 2\pi/\kappa_{\text{Rindler}} = \beta \hbar$ at inverse temperature $\beta = 2\pi/(\hbar \kappa_{\text{Rindler}})$). By the Unruh effect (Unruh 1976, "Notes on black-hole evaporation," Phys. Rev. D **14**, 870–892), the vacuum $\Omega$ is a KMS state with respect to the boost-generated flow at the Unruh temperature $T_U = \hbar a / (2\pi c k_B)$ for proper acceleration $a$. The modular flow identification therefore recovers the Connes–Rovelli Thermal Time Hypothesis (Connes and Rovelli 1994, "Von Neumann algebra automorphisms and time-thermodynamics relation in generally covariant quantum theories," Class. Quantum Grav. **11**, 2899–2917) as derived structure — the Wick-rotated-$x_4$-translation reading of §28.6 of the present paper, with the McGucken-Wick coordinate identification as the coordinate bridge.*

*(vii) **(Relative modular operator and Araki relative entropy on the Sphere-cogenerated wedge algebra)** For any two faithful normal states $\varphi, \psi$ on $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$ with representing vectors $\Phi, \Psi \in \mathcal{P}$, the relative modular operator $\Delta_{\Psi|\Phi}$ exists and is unique by the Araki 1973 construction. The Araki relative entropy*
$$S(\varphi \| \psi) \;=\; -\langle\Phi \,|\, \log \Delta_{\Psi|\Phi} \,|\, \Phi\rangle$$
*(Araki 1976, Eq. (1-1), p. 809; the finite-dimensional reduction is Eq. (1-2) on the same page) is thereby a derived quantity on the Sphere-cogenerated wedge algebra, with all four modular objects $(\mathcal{M}(W_R), \mathcal{H}, J, \mathcal{P})$ supplied by $dx_4/dt = ic$: the von-Neumann algebra of the wedge $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$ via the Haag–Kastler net on the Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert space, the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ via the Minkowski-space / Hilbert-space cogeneration, the modular conjugation $J$ via the Bisognano–Wichmann identification as PT (parity-time) reflection through $p$, and the natural positive cone $\mathcal{P}$ via the standard form of Haagerup 1975. The type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ limit (restriction to a finite-dimensional subalgebra of $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$) reduces $S(\varphi\|\psi)$ to the Umegaki form of Theorem 22.3 Step 5, closing the extension from the finite-dimensional Line-B / Line-A entropy to the full type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ setting that algebraic quantum field theory requires at horizons and wedges.*

**Proof of Theorem 22.3.9.** Six steps.

*Step 1 (Wedge algebra and Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert space, giving (i)).* By the Minkowski-space / Hilbert-space cogeneration of [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, §§III-IV], $dx_4/dt = ic$ generates the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and the Haag–Kastler net $O \mapsto \mathcal{M}(O)$ of local von Neumann algebras indexed by open spacetime regions $O \subset \mathcal{M}_G$. For the right Rindler wedge $W_R(p)$, the algebra $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$ is a factor of Murray–von Neumann type $\mathrm{III}$ by Araki 1964 (free-field case: *Prog. Theor. Phys.* **32**, 956–965) refined to type $\mathrm{III}_1$ by Fredenhagen 1985 (*Commun. Math. Phys.* **97** (1), 79–89, "On the modular structure of local algebras of observables"): Fredenhagen shows that in any asymptotically scale-invariant quantum field theory the spectrum of the modular operators $\Delta$ of all local observable algebras equals the full positive real line $\mathbb{R}_+^*$ — this is the Connes 1973 type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ invariant $T(\mathcal{M}) = \mathbb{R}$ characterizing the hyperfinite type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ factor. The result is extended to the universal structure of local algebras by Buchholz–D'Antoni–Fredenhagen 1987 (*Commun. Math. Phys.* **111** (1), 123–135, "The universal structure of local algebras"). The type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ character is the Araki–Fredenhagen field-algebra classification; it is independent of the Sphere-cogeneration route and holds in any Wightman theory with a Reeh–Schlieder vacuum. This establishes (i).

*Step 2 (Reeh–Schlieder from $dx_4/dt = ic$, giving (ii)).* The Reeh–Schlieder theorem (Reeh and Schlieder 1961, *Nuovo Cimento* **22**, 1051–1068, Theorem 1) states that for any Wightman theory with vacuum $\Omega$ invariant under the Poincaré representation $U$, and for any open spacetime region $O$ with non-empty interior, $\mathcal{M}(O)\Omega$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ and $\Omega$ is separating for $\mathcal{M}(O)$. The Wightman axioms (spectrum condition, locality, vacuum uniqueness) are derived theorems of $dx_4/dt = ic$ via the Minkowski-space / Hilbert-space cogeneration [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, Theorem 10]. The locality axiom follows from the null-cone causal order generated by the $x_4 = ict$ coordinate structure (Theorem 3 of the present paper). The spectrum condition (positive energy) follows from the $+ic$ orientation of the Principle. Vacuum uniqueness follows from the irreducibility of the Poincaré representation on the Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert space. The Reeh–Schlieder cyclic-separating property is therefore a derived consequence of $dx_4/dt = ic$ via these three derived axioms. This establishes (ii).

*Step 3 (Standard form, giving (iii)).* By Haagerup 1975 (*Math. Scand.* **37**, 271–283, Theorem 1.6), every von Neumann algebra admits a standard form, unique up to unitary equivalence. Applied to $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$ with cyclic separating vacuum $\Omega$ (Step 2), the standard form $(\mathcal{M}(W_R), \mathcal{H}, J, \mathcal{P})$ exists and is unique. The Tomita operator $S_\Omega$ is defined by closure of $a\Omega \mapsto a^*\Omega$ for $a \in \mathcal{M}(W_R)$; its polar decomposition $S_\Omega = J \Delta_\Omega^{1/2}$ identifies $J$ and $\Delta_\Omega$ (Araki 1974, *Pacific J. Math.* **50**, 309–354, §3). This establishes (iii).

*Step 4 (Bisognano–Wichmann identification, giving (iv) and (v)).* The Bisognano–Wichmann theorem is proved in Bisognano and Wichmann 1975 (*J. Math. Phys.* **16**, 985–1007, Theorems 1 and 2) for the free Hermitian scalar field and extended in Bisognano and Wichmann 1976 (*J. Math. Phys.* **17**, 303–321, Theorem 1) to all Wightman fields satisfying the Wightman axioms plus the additional analyticity condition from the Reeh–Schlieder theorem. The theorem's statement: for the vacuum state $\Omega$ on the right Rindler wedge algebra $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$, the modular operator satisfies $\Delta_\Omega^{it} = U(\Lambda_{x^1}(-2\pi t))$ and the modular conjugation satisfies $J = \Theta \cdot R_1(\pi)$, where $U, \Lambda_{x^1}, \Theta, R_1$ are as in (iv). Under $dx_4/dt = ic$, the $x^0$-component of the geometric reflection $(x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3) \mapsto (-x^0, -x^1, x^2, x^3)$ embedded in $\Theta$ corresponds to the $x_4$-reflection $x_4 \mapsto -x_4$ via the Minkowski coordinate relation $x_4 = ict$ and the McGucken-Wick identification $\tau_W = x_4/c$ ([McWick, Theorem 30.9.2]). The $x_4 \mapsto -x_4$ reflection is the operation that swaps $\Sigma_+(p)$ and $\Sigma_-(p)$; the geometric exclusion of $\Sigma_-(p)$ by $+ic$ (Theorem 3 property (c) of the present paper) renders $J$ as the formal single-Sphere PT reflection through $p$. This establishes (iv) and (v).

*Step 5 (Modular flow as Wick-rotated $x_4$-translation and Unruh KMS, giving (vi)).* The modular flow $\sigma_t^\Omega(a) = \Delta_\Omega^{it} a \Delta_\Omega^{-it} = U(\Lambda_{x^1}(-2\pi t)) a U(\Lambda_{x^1}(2\pi t))$ by Step 4. Under the McGucken-Wick coordinate identification $\tau_W = x_4/c$, the Minkowski boost $\Lambda_{x^1}(s)$ in the $(x^0, x^1)$-plane is the Wick rotation (angle $is$) of the Euclidean rotation $R_{(\tau_W, x^1)}(s)$ in the $(\tau_W, x^1)$-plane. For boost parameter $s = -2\pi t$, this is the Euclidean rotation by angle $2\pi t$ in the $(\tau_W, x^1)$-plane, closing on itself at $t = 1$. The closure period in $\tau_W$ is $\tau_W = 2\pi / \kappa_{\text{Rindler}}$ where $\kappa_{\text{Rindler}}$ is the surface gravity of the Rindler horizon, giving KMS periodicity $\tau_W = \beta \hbar$ at Unruh inverse temperature $\beta = 2\pi / (\hbar \kappa_{\text{Rindler}})$. By the Unruh effect (Unruh 1976, *Phys. Rev. D* **14**, 870–892; Theorem 17 of the present paper), the vacuum $\Omega$ is a KMS state at the Unruh temperature $T_U = \hbar a / (2\pi c k_B)$ for proper acceleration $a$ of the wedge observer. The identification of modular flow with Wick-rotated $x_4$-translation is the Connes–Rovelli Thermal Time Hypothesis (*Class. Quantum Grav.* **11**, 2899–2917) recovered as derived structure per §28.6 of the present paper, with the McGucken-Wick coordinate identification $\tau_W = x_4/c$ as the coordinate bridge. For a Schwarzschild horizon, the boost reduces to the horizon-generating Killing vector and $T_U$ reduces to the Hawking temperature $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$ (Theorem 16 of the present paper, independent derivation via Euclidean cigar closure under the McGucken-Wick rotation). *Step 6 (Relative modular operator and Araki entropy on the Sphere-cogenerated wedge algebra, giving (vii)).* For two faithful normal states $\varphi, \psi$ on $\mathcal{M}(W_R)$, the Araki 1973 construction (*Publ. RIMS Kyoto Univ.* **9**, 165–209) defines the relative Tomita operator $S_{\Psi|\Phi}$ by closing the map $a\Phi \mapsto a^*\Psi$ for $a \in \mathcal{M}(W_R)$ on the cyclic subspace $\mathcal{M}(W_R)\Phi$ (dense in $\mathcal{H}$ by Step 2). (1-1), p. 809, in the Introduction §1) is then well-defined on the Sphere-cogenerated wedge algebra, with all four standard-form objects supplied by $dx_4/dt = ic$ via Steps 1–5. The Araki 1977 (*Publ. RIMS Kyoto Univ.* **13** (1), 173–192, "Relative Entropy for States of von Neumann Algebras II") properties — non-negativity (Theorem 3.6(1): $S(\varphi/\psi) \geq 0$ when $\varphi(1) = \psi(1) > 0$, with equality iff $\varphi = \psi$), joint lower semi-continuity (Theorem 3.7(1): under norm convergence of $\varphi_\alpha, \psi_\alpha$, $\liminf S(\varphi_\alpha/\psi_\alpha) \geq S(\varphi/\psi)$), joint convexity (Theorem 3.8(1)), and reduction to the Umegaki form in the type-$\mathrm{I}_n$ case (via Eq. (1.1) and (1.2) of §1 of Araki 1976, giving $S(\varphi/\psi) = \varphi(\log\rho_\varphi - \log\rho_\psi)$ in the finite-dimensional factor setting) — follow from the Araki 1976 definition applied to the Sphere-cogenerated standard form. Rep.* **14** (2), 59–85, "Conditional expectation in an operator algebra, IV (entropy and information)") $S(\varphi\|\psi) = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_\varphi \log\rho_\varphi - \rho_\varphi \log\rho_\psi)$, the Line-B entropy of Theorem 22.3 Step 5 cited at reference [481] and the Line-A entropy cited at reference [476]. This establishes (vii) and completes the proof of Theorem 22.3.9. $\blacksquare$

### 22.3.10 Uhlmann 1977 monotonicity of the Araki relative entropy under completely positive unital normal maps — the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ data-processing inequality derived from the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Haar-measure contraction under coarse-graining of the McGucken Sphere

**McGucken Principle anchor.** Under $dx_4/dt = ic$ the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ at every event $p$ carries the unique $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant Haar probability measure $\mu_H$ (Theorem 7 of the present paper, via Haar's 1933 uniqueness theorem on the homogeneous space $S^2 = \mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{SO}(2)$), with the Compton wavelength $\lambda_C = h/(mc)$ setting the resolution scale at which $x_4$-advance modes on the Sphere are counted. Any coarse-graining of the Sphere — a measurable projection to a subset of distinguishable $x_4$-advance modes, or more generally a completely positive (CP) unital normal map between wedge algebras generated by McGucken Spheres at distinct events — contracts the Haar-measure-weighted mode distribution to a less-informative distribution on the coarse-grained Sphere. The Uhlmann 1977 monotonicity of the Araki relative entropy under CP unital normal maps is the corresponding statement at the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ operator-algebraic level: coarse-graining the Sphere cannot increase the state-distinguishability measured by the Araki relative entropy of Theorem 22.3.9 Step 6. This is the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ data-processing inequality generalizing the Lindblad 1975 monotonicity of the Umegaki relative entropy under CP maps on finite-dimensional matrix algebras.

**Uhlmann's theorem (statement).** Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ be von Neumann algebras, and let $\alpha : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}$ be a 2-positive unital normal map (every completely positive unital normal map is 2-positive unital, so this condition is weaker than complete positivity; the full-CP case is the operationally relevant one in quantum information). Let $\varphi, \psi$ be faithful normal states on $\mathcal{M}$ with pullbacks $\varphi \circ \alpha, \psi \circ \alpha$ on $\mathcal{N}$. Then
$$\boxed{\; S(\varphi \circ \alpha \,\|\, \psi \circ \alpha) \;\leq\; S(\varphi \,\|\, \psi).\;}$$
This is Uhlmann's theorem, from Uhlmann 1977, "Relative entropy and the Wigner–Yanase–Dyson–Lieb concavity in an interpolation theory," *Commun. Math. Phys.* **54** (1), 21–32, Theorem 1.2.

**Theorem 22.3.10 (Uhlmann monotonicity derived from $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Haar-measure contraction under coarse-graining of the McGucken Sphere).** *Under $dx_4/dt = ic$, any CP unital normal map $\alpha : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}$ between wedge algebras generated by McGucken Spheres at events $q, p$ respectively induces a measure-theoretic contraction $\alpha^* : \mathcal{P}(\Sigma_+(p)) \to \mathcal{P}(\Sigma_+(q))$ on the respective $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Haar probability measures (where $\mathcal{P}(\Sigma)$ denotes the space of probability measures on $\Sigma$ absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_H$). The contraction is monotone-decreasing on the Araki relative entropy of state-pairs:*
$$S(\varphi \circ \alpha \,\|\, \psi \circ \alpha) \;\leq\; S(\varphi \,\|\, \psi)$$
*for all faithful normal state-pairs $\varphi, \psi$ on $\mathcal{M}$. The equality holds iff $\alpha$ is a sufficient subalgebra inclusion in the Petz 1986 sense (Petz, "Sufficient subalgebras and the relative entropy of states of a von Neumann algebra," Commun. Math. Phys. **105**, 123–131, Theorem 2.1), equivalently iff the Sphere-level coarse-graining preserves all distinguishability between $\mu_H^\varphi$ and $\mu_H^\psi$.*

**Proof of Theorem 22.3.10.** Four steps.

*Step 1 (Stinespring dilation of the CP unital normal map).* Every CP unital normal map $\alpha : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}$ admits a Stinespring dilation (Stinespring 1955, "Positive functions on $C^*$-algebras," *Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.* **6**, 211–216, Theorem 1): there exist a Hilbert space $\mathcal{K}$, a bounded isometry $V : \mathcal{H}_\mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{H}_\mathcal{N} \otimes \mathcal{K}$, and a $*$-representation $\pi : \mathcal{N} \to B(\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{N} \otimes \mathcal{K})$ such that
$$\alpha(a) = V^* \pi(a) V \quad \text{for all } a \in \mathcal{N}.$$
Under Theorem 22.3.9 (Step 1), both $\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{H}_\mathcal{N}$ are Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert spaces for the Spheres at events $p$ and $q$ respectively, so the Stinespring isometry $V$ corresponds to a measurable embedding of the $x_4$-advance mode structure of $\Sigma_+(p)$ into the enlarged mode structure of $\Sigma_+(q)$ coupled to an auxiliary Hilbert space $\mathcal{K}$ (the ``environment'' in quantum-information language).

*Step 2 ($\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Haar contraction on the Sphere level).* The Haar measure $\mu_H$ on $\Sigma_+(p)$ is the unique $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant probability measure on the two-sphere $S^2 = \mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{SO}(2)$ by Haar's 1933 uniqueness theorem (Haar, "Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen," *Ann. of Math.* **34**, 147–169). For any measurable map $\pi : \Sigma_+(p) \to \Sigma_+(q)$ induced by the Stinespring dilation of Step 1 (pushforward of $x_4$-advance modes from $p$ to $q$ composed with the auxiliary coupling), the pushforward measures $\pi_* \mu_H^\varphi, \pi_* \mu_H^\psi$ on $\Sigma_+(q)$ (defined by $\pi_* \mu_H^\xi(E) = \mu_H^\xi(\pi^{-1}(E))$ for measurable $E \subset \Sigma_+(q)$) satisfy the classical data-processing inequality for the Kullback–Leibler divergence (standard measure-theoretic result; cf. Kullback 1959, *Information Theory and Statistics*, Chapter 2):
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_* \mu_H^\varphi \,\|\, \pi_* \mu_H^\psi) \;\leq\; D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu_H^\varphi \,\|\, \mu_H^\psi),$$
where $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu \| \nu) = \int \log(d\mu/d\nu) \, d\mu$ for mutually absolutely continuous measures $\mu, \nu$. The inequality is strict unless $\pi$ is injective modulo $\mu_H^\varphi$-null and $\mu_H^\psi$-null sets. This is the Sphere-level contraction derived from the Haar-measure structure of $\Sigma_+(p)$ via $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariance.

*Step 3 (Lifting from Sphere-level classical measure to Araki operator-algebraic entropy via Uhlmann's interpolation argument).* Uhlmann 1977 (*Commun. Math. Phys.* **54**, 21–32) proves monotonicity of the Araki relative entropy under 2-positive unital normal maps via the interpolation-theory characterization of relative entropy — specifically, Uhlmann shows that the Araki relative entropy $S(\varphi\|\psi)$ equals the Wigner–Yanase–Dyson–Lieb concave functional (Lieb 1973, "Convex trace functions and the Wigner–Yanase–Dyson conjecture," *Advances in Mathematics* **11**, 267–288) evaluated at the Connes cocycle derivative $(D\varphi : D\psi)_t$ of the two states. The monotonicity under 2-positive unital normal maps $\alpha$ then follows from the Stinespring dilation (Step 1) combined with the concavity of the Lieb functional and the monotonicity of the classical Kullback–Leibler divergence under the pushforward of Step 2. Specifically, Uhlmann's argument reduces the operator-algebraic monotonicity to the classical measure-theoretic monotonicity by passing to the Connes cocycle derivative and applying the Lieb concavity theorem. Under $dx_4/dt = ic$, the classical measure-theoretic monotonicity of Step 2 is the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Haar-measure contraction on the Sphere, so Uhlmann's interpolation argument lifts the Sphere-level contraction to the type-$\mathrm{III}_1$ Araki-entropy monotonicity on the wedge algebra:
$$S(\varphi \circ \alpha \,\|\, \psi \circ \alpha) \;\leq\; S(\varphi \,\|\, \psi).$$

*Step 4 (Equality case via Petz sufficiency).* Petz 1986 (*Commun. Math. Phys.* **105**, 123–131, Theorem 2.1) proves that equality $S(\varphi \circ \alpha \|\psi \circ \alpha) = S(\varphi\|\psi)$ holds iff $\alpha$ is a sufficient subalgebra inclusion in the sense that there exists a CP unital map $\beta : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}$ with $\alpha \circ \beta = \mathrm{id}_\mathcal{M}$ on both $\varphi$ and $\psi$ (equivalently, $\alpha$ is a $\varphi$- and $\psi$-recovery map). Under $dx_4/dt = ic$, Petz sufficiency corresponds to Sphere-level reversibility: the Sphere-level coarse-graining $\pi$ of Step 2 preserves all distinguishability between $\mu_H^\varphi$ and $\mu_H^\psi$ iff $\pi$ is injective modulo null sets, which iff the Sphere-level KL divergence is preserved under pushforward. The equality case therefore holds iff the Sphere-level coarse-graining is reversible on the states in question. This completes the proof of Theorem 22.3.10. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary 22.3.A (Casini 2008 Bekenstein bound as a derived theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ via Theorem 22.3.9).** *Casini 2008 (Casini, "Relative entropy and the Bekenstein bound," Class. Quantum Grav. **25**, 205021) derives the Bekenstein bound on the entropy of a localized excitation of radius $R$ and energy $E$ above the vacuum,*
$$S(\rho_V) - S(\rho_V^0) \;\leq\; \mathrm{tr}(K \rho_V) - \mathrm{tr}(K \rho_V^0) \;=\; \lambda \, R \, E / (\hbar c),$$
*with $\lambda = \pi$ for ball-shaped regions (Casini 2008, Eqs. (1) and (9)) and $\lambda = 2\pi$ for the orthodox Bekenstein 1981 Rindler-wedge form,*

Casini 2008 Eq. (17), rearranged from $S(\rho_V \| \rho_V^0) \geq 0$ (Araki 1977, Theorem 3.6(1)) on the ball-region algebra, gives*

*with $K = -\log\rho_V^0$ the vacuum modular Hamiltonian for the ball. Casini's Eq. (9) gives $K$ in closed form,*
$$K \;=\; 2\pi \int_0^R dr \int r^2 \, d\Omega \; \frac{R^2 - r^2}{2R} \; H(r,\theta,\phi,0),$$
*with $H$ the CFT energy density on the ball interior (Hislop and Longo 1982, Commun. Math. Phys. **84** (1), 71–85, DOI 10.1007/BF01208372). Under Theorem 22.3.9, every object in the inequality — $S(\rho_V\|\rho_V^0)$, $\mathcal{M}(V)$, $\omega$, $K$, and the Hislop–Longo form — is derived from $dx_4/dt = ic$ via the Sphere-cogenerated standard form, so the Casini derivation is a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ through Theorem 22.3.9. This extends Theorem 15 of the present paper: Theorem 15 derives the horizon-area form $S_{BH} = k_B A/(4\ell_P^2)$ by Planck-sphere tiling; Corollary 22.3.A derives the Bekenstein inequality for localized excitations by Araki-entropy positivity.*

**Corollary 22.3.B (Faulkner–Guica–Hartman–Myers–Van Raamsdonk 2014 linearized Einstein equations from the entanglement first law as a derived theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ via Theorem 22.3.9).** *Faulkner, Guica, Hartman, Myers, and Van Raamsdonk 2014 (JHEP **03**, 051) derive the linearized Einstein equations from the first-law variation of the entanglement entropy on ball-shaped regions in a holographic conformal field theory:*

*where $K_V$ is the modular Hamiltonian for the ball-region vacuum, combined with the Ryu–Takayanagi 2006 formula (Ryu and Takayanagi, "Holographic derivation of entanglement entropy from AdS/CFT," Phys. Rev. Lett. **96**, 181602) $S_{\text{EE}}(V) = \mathrm{Area}(\tilde V)/(4 G_N)$ relating the boundary-CFT entanglement entropy to the bulk-AdS extremal-surface area $\tilde V$ with $G_N$ the bulk Newton constant. Under Theorem 15 of the present paper and the holographic restatement of Theorem 19.4 (Hilbert–Jacobson Agreement), the Ryu–Takayanagi formula $S_{\text{EE}} = A/(4G_N)$ is the holographic reading of Planck-sphere tiling. The full non-linear extension (Faulkner, Haehl, Hijano, Parrikar, Rabideau, and Van Raamsdonk 2017, "Nonlinear gravity from entanglement in CFTs," JHEP **08**, 057) and the Jafferis–Lewkowycz–Maldacena–Suh 2016 result (Jafferis, Lewkowycz, Maldacena, and Suh, "Relative entropy equals bulk relative entropy," JHEP **06**, 004) stating that boundary-CFT relative entropy equals bulk-AdS relative entropy under the holographic duality lift to the McGucken $dx_4/dt = ic$ framework in the same way: both are statements about the Sphere-cogenerated Araki relative entropy's behavior under the Sphere-level duality that generates the AdS/CFT correspondence as a derived consequence ([MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, §V, holographic reduction of the Sphere-cogenerated Haag–Kastler net]).*

## Theorem 22.4: Minkowski Space and Hilbert Space Are Both High-Entropy Coarse-Grainings of the McGucken Sphere — the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Reading of the Carcassi–Landini–Aidala (2026) Classical-Limit-as-High-Entropy Result

### 22.4.1 Statement of the theorem

Under the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ — the fourth dimension physically expanding at rate $c$ from every spacetime event — both Minkowski space and Hilbert-space Born density are higher-entropy readings of the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$, obtained by coarse-graining away (respectively) the $x_4$-cycle structure and the phase structure of the wavefront. Both coarse-grainings are entropy-increasing in the Carcassi–Landini–Aidala (2026) [492] sense: each discards a distinguishable degree of freedom of the Sphere and thereby raises the state-count-in-$\hbar$-units entropy $S = k_B \ln \Omega$ by exactly the log of the collapsed alternatives. The McGucken Sphere is the low-entropy fully-resolved object of which Minkowski space and the Hilbert-space Born density are the two high-entropy shadows. The chain is:

$$\underbrace{\Sigma_+(p) \text{ at every event}}_{\text{low-entropy: cycles and phase resolved}} \xrightarrow{\;\;\text{coarse-grain cycles}\;\;} \underbrace{\mathcal{M}_4 = (t, \vec x); \; x_4 = ict}_{\text{high-entropy: Minkowski geometry}}$$

$$\underbrace{\Sigma_+(p) \text{ at every event}}_{\text{low-entropy: cycles and phase resolved}} \xrightarrow{\;\;\text{coarse-grain phase}\;\;} \underbrace{|\psi(\vec x)|^2 \text{ on rays}}_{\text{high-entropy: Born density}}$$

The identification is rigorous at the scope of these two specific coarse-grainings (of cycles and of phase); it is not a claim that every kind of concealment reduces to thermodynamic entropy. The scope is fixed in §22.4.7.

### 22.4.2 The Carcassi–Landini–Aidala (2026) result — verbatim record of what is being read

Carcassi, Landini, and Aidala [492] (*Classical mechanics as the high-entropy limit of quantum mechanics*, Physica Scripta **101**, 065105, 2026; arXiv:2411.00972v3) establish four results that ground the reading of the McGucken Sphere developed in this theorem.

**Result 1 (main thesis, verbatim).** "Classical mechanics can be recovered as the high-entropy limit of quantum mechanics. That is, the high entropy masks quantum effects, and mixed states of high enough entropy can be approximated with classical distributions."

**Result 2 (the $\hbar$-as-counting-unit identification, verbatim from §1).** "Entropy is the logarithm for the count of states, which is quantified in units of $\hbar$. Therefore, taking $\hbar \to 0$ is equivalent to setting the entropy for pure states to $-\infty$."

**Result 3 (the entropic aliasing mechanism, verbatim from §2.3).** In the two-slit setup: "The case where we randomize the phase is indistinguishable from the case where we randomize the path. In other words, uncertainty over a quantum feature behaves like uncertainty over a classical feature, regardless of the source of the uncertainty." And in the Bloch ball: "states at equal entropy form a series of concentric spheres. As we increase the entropy, the points of these spheres become closer and closer, and therefore the error in using a mixture of $|L\rangle$ and $|R\rangle$ instead of the actual state becomes smaller."

**Result 4 (the pure quantum stretching map, §4.3).** The map $T_Q$ realised as the Lindblad evolution with $H = 0$, jump operator $L = a^\dagger$, and rate $\gamma$, acts on the canonical commutator as $[T_Q(X), T_Q(P)] = \lambda i\hbar$ with $\lambda = e^{\gamma t}$. Redefining $\hat X = X/\sqrt\lambda$, $\hat P = P/\sqrt\lambda$ gives $[\hat X, \hat P] = i\hbar/\lambda$, so $\lambda \to \infty$ is mathematically identical to $\hbar \to 0$. This is the Moyal-to-Poisson group contraction realised as an entropy increase.

**Closing open question (§5, verbatim).** "We wonder whether it can be proven that quantum mechanics is the only way to fix the low-entropy range of classical mechanics. That is, is quantum mechanics the only theory that can recover classical mechanics at high entropy?"

Carcassi–Landini–Aidala emphasise that Result 1 is "independent of possible underlying mechanisms and of what interpretation is chosen for both quantum states and entropy." The McGucken framework supplies a specific physical mechanism consistent with the result; the four subsections below record what that mechanism looks like.

### 22.4.3 The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies the physical referent for $\hbar$ that Carcassi treats abstractly

The McGucken Principle — $dx_4/dt = ic$ at every event of $\mathcal{M}_G$ — carries a specific physical reading of $\hbar$: on the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$, $\hbar$ is the action per Compton cycle of the wavefront. For a particle of rest energy $mc^2$ Compton-coupled to the Sphere at $p$ (Theorem 4 of the present paper), the Compton period is $T_C = h/(mc^2)$ and the Compton wavelength is $\lambda_C = h/(mc)$; $\hbar$ is the reduced action $E \cdot T_C / (2\pi) = h/(2\pi)$ per cycle. In this reading, $\hbar$ is not a free abstract parameter — it is the wavelength/action attribute of the physical wavefront, paired with $c$ (the rate attribute) as the two constants of the one Sphere-expansion.

**The physical meaning of $\hbar \to 0$ in the framework.** Carcassi's Result 2 states that $\hbar \to 0$ corresponds mathematically to setting the pure-state zero of entropy to $-\infty$. In the McGucken reading, the same limit has a direct geometric meaning: the Sphere's cycle-wavelength $\lambda_C = h/(mc)$ shrinks to zero relative to the scales being probed, so the discrete $x_4$-advance cycles become individually unresolved and the wavefront looks continuous. The abstract "state count in $\hbar$ units" of Carcassi becomes the count of Compton-cycle-resolved states on the Sphere; taking $\hbar \to 0$ is taking the resolution to a scale where the cycles alias into a continuum.

**The physical meaning of the ${\hbar \leftrightarrow c}$ parallel.** Carcassi's Result 1 notes an explicit formal analogy: $\hbar \to 0$ (classical limit) is parallel to $c \to \infty$ (non-relativistic limit), and each is "independent of underlying mechanism." The McGucken framework grounds this parallel: $c$ and $\hbar$ are the two constants of the same physical wavefront — $c$ its expansion rate, $\hbar$ its cycle-wavelength — so both limits are limits of the one Sphere-expansion, taken along different attributes of it. The formal analogy Carcassi records is a consequence of the physical fact that both constants describe attributes of a single geometric object.

McGucken's contribution here: a physical referent for $\hbar$ (Sphere wavelength) that grounds Carcassi's abstract counting unit, and a physical unification of the $\hbar \to 0$ and $c \to \infty$ limits as two limits on the two attributes of the one Sphere.

### 22.4.4 Minkowski space as the high-entropy coarse-graining of the $x_4$-cycles

The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ generates the physical fourth-axis expansion at every event, with the $x_4$-advance realised through discrete Compton cycles for every Compton-coupled particle sector (Theorem 4 of the present paper). Minkowski space $\mathcal{M}_4$ is the coordinate integration of this expansion: $x_4 = \int ic \, dt = ict$. This coordinate integration is a coarse-graining in the Carcassi–Landini–Aidala sense.

**The coarse-graining, precisely.** For a worldline of proper time $\tau = t/\gamma$ that has undergone $N = t/T_C = t \cdot mc^2/h$ Compton cycles in coordinate time $t$, the Sphere resolves $N$ distinguishable cycle-states (the position of the cycle-phase at each event along the worldline). Minkowski space $\mathcal{M}_4$ integrates over the cycle-phase: only the coordinate $x_4 = ict$ is retained, not the cycle-count structure within it. The $N$ distinguishable cycle-states collapse to a single continuous-coordinate label. This is exactly Carcassi's Result 3 mechanism (entropic aliasing): $N$ distinguishable microstates become indistinguishable in the coarse-grained description.

**The entropy increase.** The state count on the Sphere with cycles resolved is $\Omega_{\text{Sphere}}$; the state count on the same Sphere with cycles integrated into a continuous $x_4$-coordinate is $\Omega_{\text{Sphere}}/N$ per unit-coordinate-cell. The Boltzmann entropy of the coordinate-integrated description exceeds the entropy of the cycle-resolved description by
$$\Delta S_{\text{Minkowski}} = k_B \ln N = k_B \ln \left(\frac{t \cdot mc^2}{h}\right) = k_B \ln\left(\frac{t}{T_C}\right),$$
which is Carcassi's Result 2 identity (entropy $= k_B$ times the log of the cycle count in $\hbar$-units of action) applied to the specific Sphere coarse-graining that produces Minkowski coordinates.

**The correspondence with Carcassi's stretching map.** Carcassi's stretching map $T_Q$ multiplies phase-space volume by $\lambda$ and raises entropy by $k_B \ln \lambda$. The Sphere-to-Minkowski coarse-graining is the specific stretching with $\lambda = N = t/T_C$ — the number of Compton cycles the coarse-graining aliases into a single coordinate cell. Minkowski geometry is the fixed point of the Sphere's expansion at the scale where all $N$ cycles have been integrated over.

McGucken's contribution here: the identification of Minkowski coordinates as the specific Sphere-coarse-graining that integrates cycles at rate $\lambda = t/T_C$; the classical-limit interpretation of the coordinate description as its Carcassi high-entropy reading.

### 22.4.5 The Hilbert-space Born density as the high-entropy coarse-graining of the phase

The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ generates the wavefunction $\psi(\vec x, t)$ as the phase-and-amplitude of the wavefront at every event (Theorem 20 of the present paper, and [MGHilbertBorn] [61]). The Born density $|\psi(\vec x, t)|^2$ is the modulus-squared of the wavefunction: the phase information $\arg \psi$ is discarded. This phase-discarding is a coarse-graining in the Carcassi–Landini–Aidala sense.

**The coarse-graining, precisely.** The wavefunction $\psi = |\psi| e^{i\varphi}$ carries both amplitude $|\psi|$ and phase $\varphi$ as distinguishable degrees of freedom; the Born density $|\psi|^2 = \psi^* \psi$ retains only the amplitude. Two wavefunctions with the same amplitude and different phases give the same Born density but different physical predictions in the interference regime: for the two-slit example of Carcassi's Result 3, the states $|+\rangle = (|L\rangle + |R\rangle)/\sqrt 2$ and $|-\rangle = (|L\rangle - |R\rangle)/\sqrt 2$ have the same amplitudes at each slit but produce interference peak versus interference valley at the screen centre. The maximally mixed state $\tfrac{1}{2}|+\rangle\langle+| + \tfrac{1}{2}|-\rangle\langle-|$ has the same reduced density as $\tfrac{1}{2}|L\rangle\langle L| + \tfrac{1}{2}|R\rangle\langle R|$: uncertainty over phase and uncertainty over path give the same Born-density outcome.

**The entropy increase.** For a wavefunction with $M$ distinguishable phase-states at the resolution being probed, the state count with phase resolved is $\Omega_{\text{wave}} = |\psi|^2 \cdot M$; the state count with phase integrated over (the Born density) is $\Omega_{\text{Born}} = |\psi|^2$. The Boltzmann entropy of the Born-density description exceeds the entropy of the wavefunction description by
$$\Delta S_{\text{Born}} = k_B \ln M,$$
which is Carcassi's Result 3 mechanism applied to the specific Sphere-coarse-graining that produces the Born density.

**The Bloch-ball reading.** Carcassi's Result 3 second component (Bloch-ball crowding) has a direct McGucken reading: the Bloch ball is the phase-quotient of the McGucken Sphere in the two-state sector (§6.2.12 of the present paper). Equal-entropy states form concentric Bloch spheres because they correspond to equal-cycle-count Sphere-states with different phases. High entropy crowds the Bloch spheres toward the maximally mixed centre because it corresponds to Sphere-states with all phases equally weighted — the phase-averaged Sphere, which is what the Born density records.

**The rigorous statement, restated with scope.** Both Minkowski space and the Hilbert-Born density are high-entropy readings of the McGucken Sphere in the Carcassi–Landini–Aidala sense, because (a) each is obtained from the Sphere by discarding a specific distinguishable degree of freedom ($x_4$-cycles for Minkowski, phase for Born density), (b) each discarded degree of freedom is exactly countable in $\hbar$-units of action, and (c) the entropy of the coarse-grained description exceeds the entropy of the Sphere at fully-resolved scale by the log of the collapsed alternatives in each case, matching Carcassi–Landini–Aidala's mechanism precisely.

### 22.5.2 The Carcassi Third-Law derivation of the classical uncertainty principle — verbatim record

Carcassi's derivation in the CORE1 lecture [493] (timecode 22:00–27:00) proceeds in four steps:

**Step 1 (dimensional-consistency requirement, verbatim from ~22:14).** The standard textbook expressions for classical entropy $S = \ln(\Delta x \Delta p)$ are dimensionally incorrect: *"X is units of length and P of units of mass times velocity. So we are taking the logarithm of a quantity with units. And this is dimensionally incorrect. You can only take the logarithm of a pure number. Similarly, $\rho$ is a probability density. So it has units of one over areas of phase space. And this is also dimensionally incorrect."* The fix requires introducing a constant $h$ of phase-space-area dimensions: $S = \ln(\Delta x \Delta p / h)$. Carcassi's physical characterisation of $h$ (verbatim from ~23:15): *"If you take a uniform distribution of a region of area $h$, then the distribution has zero entropy. $h/h$ is one and the logarithm of one is zero... $h$ is the area that corresponds to the zero of our entropy for a uniform distribution."*

**Step 2 (Gaussian upper bound on entropy at fixed uncertainty).** For a fixed uncertainty $\sigma_x \sigma_p$, the entropy $S$ is bounded above by the Gaussian-state entropy:
$$S \leq \ln\left(\frac{2\pi e \sigma_x \sigma_p}{h}\right).$$
Solving for the uncertainty gives $\sigma_x \sigma_p \geq (h/2\pi e) \cdot e^S = (\hbar/e) \cdot e^S$.

**Step 3 (Third Law of Thermodynamics: $S \geq 0$).** The Third Law of Thermodynamics (Nernst 1906, refined Planck 1911) states that entropy is bounded below: $S \geq 0$ for any physical system. Carcassi's verbatim (~19:23): *"The third law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a system cannot be lower than the one of a perfect crystalline substance. A zero entropy."*

**Step 4 (combining Steps 2 and 3, verbatim from ~25:14).** *"The exponential of zero is one. So classical statistical mechanics plus the third law of thermodynamics gives us the classical uncertainty principle. Sigma X sigma P is greater than $H$ bar over $e$. Isn't it neat?"* Formally:
$$\sigma_x \sigma_p \geq \frac{\hbar}{e} \approx 0.368 \, \hbar.$$

**Comparison with the quantum uncertainty principle.** The Heisenberg bound $\sigma_x \sigma_p \geq \hbar/2 = 0.5 \, \hbar$ is *tighter* (larger lower bound) than the classical Third-Law bound by a factor $e/2 \approx 1.36$. Carcassi's verbatim (~26:04): *"Pure states in quantum mechanics have zero entropy. So you can have lower entropy in quantum mechanics. It's like quantum mechanics takes the third law very serious. Classical mechanics doesn't. Classical mechanics does not obey the laws of thermodynamics."*

**Carcassi's remark on originality (verbatim ~25:41).** *"What I don't understand, I've never found this in the literature. I presented a few times at conference. Nobody told me, 'Ah, so and so showed this in 1936.' Like seriously, nobody figured this out before me. And if somebody did, why isn't this in every quantum textbook? It's bizarre either way."*

### 22.5.3 The McGucken Sphere reading — $\hbar$ as Sphere action-per-cycle grounds the $h$ Carcassi introduces from dimensional consistency

The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ carries a specific physical reading of the constant $h$ Carcassi introduces from dimensional consistency alone: it is the action per Compton cycle of the wavefront generated by the Principle at every event. The zero of entropy at $\Delta x \Delta p = h$ corresponds physically to the state resolvable at exactly one-cycle precision on the Sphere.

**What this contributes to Carcassi's derivation.** Carcassi obtains the constant $h$ from dimensional analysis plus the Third Law, without needing to say what $h$ physically is; his derivation of $\sigma_x \sigma_p \geq \hbar/e$ is complete without any commitment to what $\hbar$ *is*. Carcassi identifies the mechanism (~26:34, verbatim): *"You minimize the uncertainty at the same entropy precisely when you have independent Gaussians for both position and momentum. That's what you can't do anymore if you have a lower bound on the entropy because if they were independent you would be able to write the joint distribution as a product of the two. But writing a joint distribution assumes you can define a region of phase space arbitrarily small which is exactly what you can do if you have a lower bound of the entropy."* In the McGucken reading: the classical bound corresponds to a distribution occupying exactly one Sphere-cycle in *each* of position and momentum independently, giving a rectangular phase-space cell of area $\hbar/e \cdot 2\pi = 2\pi \hbar / e$.
