### 22.5.18 The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Reading of the Gibbs Paradox as Diagnostic Case 10 — the Discontinuous Entropy of Mixing $2Nk_B\ln 2$ Between Same-Species and Different-Species Gases as a Theorem of Shared McGucken-Sphere Geometry, with the Full Historical Arc from Gibbs 1875 through the 2018 *Entropy* Special Issue and the Yadin–Morris–Adesso 2021 Quantum Gibbs Paradox, the Diathermal-Partition Sphere-Transmission Mechanism, and the Exchange-Entanglement Symmetrization Postulate as the Quantum-Mechanical Content of Gibbs's Generic-Phase Count

The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ states that the fourth dimension is expanding at the invariant velocity of light $c$ in a spherically symmetric manner from every spacetime event, with the imaginary unit $i$ marking perpendicularity to the three ordinary spatial dimensions. The two Channels of the McGucken Duality read this Principle in two aspects: the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel reads the real-rate-at-$c$ aspect (the physically-real spherically-symmetric wavefront's spatial spreading, the source of entropy increase and thermodynamic dissipation); the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel reads the perpendicularity-marker-$i$ aspect (the operator-algebra apparatus that Stone's theorem generates from the one-parameter group $\exp(-i \hat H t/\hbar)$ acting on the McGucken-Sphere-cogenerated Hilbert space). This subsection establishes Diagnostic Case 10 — the Gibbs paradox — as a direct theorem of shared McGucken-Sphere geometry, with the full historical arc from Gibbs 1875 through the 2018 *Entropy* special issue and the 2021 Yadin–Morris–Adesso quantum Gibbs paradox, reading the paradox and its 148-year debate history as an extended registration of the shared-Sphere-geometry mode-count collapse that the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies as the physical mechanism.

**Statement of the Gibbs paradox in its two forms (Gibbs 1875, 1902).** The Gibbs paradox appears in two distinct forms in Gibbs's own writings, and every modern research contribution addresses one or both of them.

*Form (I) — the discontinuous drop of the entropy of mixing at species identity.* Mix two ideal gases $A$ and $B$ of equal amounts at the same temperature $T$ and same pressure $P$ through the removal of a partition separating equal half-volumes. Standard classical calculation gives the entropy of mixing
$$\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 2Nk_B \ln 2$$
independent of how similar $A$ and $B$ are chemically. As $A \to B$ continuously through some parameter (mass, molecular structure, isotopic composition, or any other continuous label), $\Delta S_{\text{mix}}$ remains at the constant value $2Nk_B\ln 2$ throughout the interpolation, then drops discontinuously to $0$ at the instant $A$ becomes exactly identical to $B$ chemically. Gibbs himself flagged this discontinuity as the puzzle in his 1875 *On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances* (Collected Works Vol. I, p. 167, footnote): verbatim from Gibbs 1875 [as recorded across the historical literature and quoted in Darrigol 2018, *Entropy* 20, 443]: *"The case is one of those in which the impossibility of an uncompensated decrease of entropy seems to be reduced to an improbability."*

*Form (II) — the non-extensivity of the naive Boltzmann phase-space entropy.* The naive Boltzmann entropy formula $S = k_B \ln \Omega$ applied to $N$ classical particles in phase-space volume $V$ gives
$$S(2N, 2V, T) = 2S(N, V, T) + 2Nk_B \ln 2$$
rather than the extensive scaling $S(2N, 2V, T) = 2S(N, V, T)$ that thermodynamic experiment requires. So combining two identical boxes of $N$ particles each in volume $V$ into one box of $2N$ particles in volume $2V$ appears to add $2Nk_B\ln 2$ to the entropy, and re-partitioning the combined box into two half-volumes of $N$ particles each appears to remove $2Nk_B\ln 2$ from the entropy — an apparent second-law violation. This is the form addressed by Gibbs's generic-phase count (formalized in *Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics*, 1902), which introduces the effective $1/N!$ factor that restores extensivity by counting permutations of same-species particles as one state rather than $N!$ distinct states.

The distinction between the two forms was made explicit by Dennis Dieks (Utrecht) in his 2018 *Entropy* contribution [Dieks 2018, *Entropy* 20, 466, verbatim]: *"A consensus seems to have developed that the Gibbs paradox in classical thermodynamics (the discontinuous drop in the entropy of mixing when the mixed gases become equal to each other) is unmysterious: in any actual situation, two gases can be separated or not, and the associated harmless discontinuity from 'yes' to 'no' is responsible for the discontinuity. By contrast, the Gibbs paradox in statistical physics continues to attract attention. Here, the problem is that standard calculations in statistical mechanics predict a non-vanishing value of the entropy of mixing even when two gases of the same kind are mixed, in conflict with thermodynamic predictions."*

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the Gibbs paradox as Diagnostic Case 10 of §22.5, with the Form (I) discontinuous-drop puzzle and the Form (II) non-extensive-entropy puzzle treated as two registrations of the same underlying physical fact — shared McGucken-Sphere geometry for same-species particles supplying a physical mechanism for the mode-count collapse that both forms record; identification of the 148-year debate history as extended registration of the shared-Sphere-geometry mode-count phenomenon that the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies as physical content.

**The pre-Gibbs record on diathermal partition permeability (Fourier 1822 through the Zeroth Law).** Before turning to Gibbs's own resolution, the historical record on partition permeability to energy exchange requires precise statement, since the Gibbs paradox rests on pre-existing thermal equilibrium across the partition — a physical fact well established by the time Gibbs writes in 1875.

*Fourier 1822.* Joseph Fourier, *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* (Firmin Didot, Paris, 1822) established the mathematical theory of heat conduction through solid walls as a continuous physical process governed by the heat equation $\partial T/\partial t = \alpha \nabla^2 T$ with thermal diffusivity $\alpha$. By 1822, the phenomenological transmission of heat through diathermal partitions is a mathematically-formalized physical process, not a puzzle. Gibbs writing in 1875 assumes the Fourier framework as established background.

*Clausius 1850s–1860s.* Rudolf Clausius, in the sequence of papers establishing the second law of thermodynamics (*Poggendorff's Annalen der Physik* 79, 368 (1850); 93, 481 (1854); 125, 353 (1865)), established the thermal-equilibrium condition: two subsystems in thermal contact through any diathermal partition reach the same temperature. This is the physical content of the second law applied to thermal contact through walls — energy flows through the wall until temperatures equalize, and thereafter the joint system is in equilibrium with a common temperature.

*Maxwell 1860, 1867.* James Clerk Maxwell's kinetic theory of gases (*Philosophical Magazine* 19, 19 (1860); 20, 21 (1860); *Philosophical Transactions* 157, 49 (1867)) treats wall-particle interactions as molecular collisions that transfer energy between the gas and the wall material. The wall is permeable to individual-molecule energy exchanges through the collision events at the wall surface. Maxwell's 1867 demon thought experiment (in the letter to P.G. Tait dated 11 December 1867, and elaborated in *Theory of Heat*, Longmans Green, London, 1871, Chapter XII) turns on this permeability: the demon operates a trapdoor precisely because the wall is otherwise the site of continuous molecule-molecule and molecule-wall energy exchanges.

*The Zeroth Law (implicit in Clausius, formalized Fowler 1931).* Ralph Fowler, in the 1931 formalization of the Zeroth Law (*Statistical Mechanics*, Cambridge University Press, 1935, with the Zeroth Law first named as such in the 1939 Fowler–Guggenheim *Statistical Thermodynamics*), stated the transitivity of thermal equilibrium: if system $A$ is in thermal equilibrium with $B$ through a diathermal partition, and $B$ is in thermal equilibrium with $C$ through another diathermal partition, then $A$ and $C$ are in thermal equilibrium. The Zeroth Law is exactly the statement that diathermal contact through a partition is a physically well-defined equilibrium-establishing relation. This is implicit in Clausius 1850s and made explicit by Fowler 1931.

*Standard textbook consensus on diathermal permeability.* By the time modern statistical mechanics textbooks are written, diathermal partition permeability is unremarked background. Max Planck, *Vorlesungen über Thermodynamik* (Veit, Leipzig, 1897), §68–70; Enrico Fermi, *Thermodynamics* (Prentice-Hall, 1937), Chapter 3; Lev Landau and Evgeny Lifshitz, *Statistical Physics* Volume 5 of the Course of Theoretical Physics (Nauka, Moscow, first Russian edition 1938; English translation Pergamon 1958), §7; Herbert Callen, *Thermodynamics* (Wiley, 1960), Chapter 2 — all treat the partition as diathermal (permeable to energy but not to particles) and take this as the working assumption of the Gibbs-paradox thought experiment. The two half-boxes are in thermal equilibrium through the partition before the partition is pulled; pulling the partition changes what the particles' center-of-mass positions can access, not whether energy exchange is possible between the two halves.

*The Maxwell-demon literature on wall-energy-exchange as the specific mechanism.* The century-long analysis of Maxwell's demon (Leo Szilard, *Zeitschrift für Physik* 53, 840 (1929); Leon Brillouin, *Journal of Applied Physics* 22, 334 (1951); Rolf Landauer, *IBM Journal of Research and Development* 5, 183 (1961); Charles Bennett, *International Journal of Theoretical Physics* 21, 905 (1982)) turns entirely on the wall being permeable to specific molecular energy exchanges while blocking bulk particle transport. The physical distinction between *diathermal permeability* (energy through) and *material impermeability* (particles blocked) is the working assumption of a century of paradox-analysis literature on partitioned gas systems.

*What the historical record has, and what it does not.* The historical record from Fourier 1822 through the Zeroth Law and standard textbooks has: (i) walls transmit energy across the partition through molecular-collision, radiative, and phonon-transport channels; (ii) thermal equilibrium across a diathermal partition is a physically-established equilibrium condition; (iii) the two half-boxes in the Gibbs setup are in thermal equilibrium through the partition before the partition is pulled; (iv) the mechanism of the energy transmission is characterized differently for different regimes (kinetic-theory molecular collisions for dilute gases, Planck 1900 blackbody radiative transfer for high-temperature cavities, Debye 1912 phonon transport for solid partitions). What the historical record does not have is: (a) a physical mechanism that unifies the collision, radiative, and phonon transport channels as one carrier; (b) a physical reason why same-species particle populations on the two sides of the partition should have their mode-counts unified into a single count while different-species populations should not. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Sphere reading supplies both — the McGucken Sphere is the common physical carrier that all three transport-channel descriptions are partial windows onto, and shared Sphere geometry for same-species particles is the physical reason for shared mode-count.

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the pre-Gibbs and post-Gibbs historical record on diathermal partition permeability (Fourier 1822 through Zeroth Law formalization by Fowler 1931, standard textbook consensus by Planck 1897, Fermi 1937, Landau–Lifshitz 1938, Callen 1960); identification of the century-long Maxwell-demon literature (Szilard 1929, Brillouin 1951, Landauer 1961, Bennett 1982) as the analytical tradition working from the diathermal-permeability-blocking-bulk-transport distinction; identification of the McGucken Sphere at rate $c$ from every event as the common physical carrier unifying the kinetic-theory collision, Planck radiative, and Debye phonon transport channels; identification of shared McGucken-Sphere geometry for same-species particles as the physical reason for shared mode-count that the historical record calls for but does not supply.

**Gibbs's own resolution — the semi-permeable membrane analysis (1875) and the generic-phase count (1902).** The historical literature persistently misreads Gibbs as having flagged the paradox and left it unresolved; the primary-source record shows Gibbs resolved both forms within his own writings, and the century-long "Gibbs paradox" debate exists largely because the 1902 *Elementary Principles* did not carry forward the 1875 resolution.

*Gibbs 1875 — the semi-permeable membrane derivation of the entropy of mixing for different gases.* In *On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances* (Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences 3, 108 (1875–1876); 3, 343 (1877–1878); Collected Works Vol. I, Longmans Green, London, 1928, pp. 55–353), Gibbs derives the entropy of mixing for two different ideal gases through the reversible-mixing thought experiment using semi-permeable membranes. The construction: a membrane transparent to species $A$ but opaque to species $B$, and a second membrane transparent to $B$ but opaque to $A$, together allow the two initially-separated gases to be reversibly interpenetrated with the extraction of work $W = 2Nk_BT \ln 2$. By the reversibility, the entropy change is $\Delta S = W/T = 2Nk_B \ln 2$, giving the entropy of mixing for two different ideal gases at equal $T$ and $P$ in equal half-volumes. The derivation rests on the physical constructibility of species-distinguishing semi-permeable membranes; if no such membrane can be constructed (because the species are identical), no reversible work extraction is possible, and no entropy of mixing is defined. Gibbs concludes that the entropy of mixing is precisely the reversibly-extractable work per unit temperature — a physical operational quantity, not a bookkeeping abstraction — and its yes/no character tracks the yes/no constructibility of species-distinguishing membranes.

*Gibbs 1875 on the discontinuity as the yes/no character of the distinguishing operation.* The Form (I) discontinuity is, for Gibbs, not a paradox but a direct consequence of the operational definition of the entropy of mixing as reversibly-extractable-work-per-temperature: species identity is a yes/no property of what distinguishing membranes are physically constructible, so the entropy of mixing inherits the yes/no character. Verbatim from Gibbs 1875 [Collected Works Vol. I, p. 167, footnote]: *"The case is one of those in which the impossibility of an uncompensated decrease of entropy seems to be reduced to an improbability."* Jaynes 1992 identifies this footnote as Gibbs's own recognition that Form (I) records a physical feature reflecting the yes/no character of species distinguishability.

*Gibbs 1902 — the generic-phase versus specific-phase count.* In *Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics* (Scribner's, New York, 1902; Yale University Press reprint 1948), Chapter XV titled "Systems Composed of Molecules," Gibbs introduces the distinction between two ways of counting states in phase space. Verbatim characterization of the distinction, as established across the Gibbs-scholarship literature and consistent with Gibbs's *Elementary Principles* Ch. XV: **specific phase** is a state of the $N$-particle system labeled by which particle is at which phase-space point (all $N!$ permutations of the $N$ particles counted as distinct states); **generic phase** is a state labeled only by how many particles are in each cell of phase space (permutations of same-species particles counted as one state). Gibbs concludes that thermodynamic entropy corresponds to the generic-phase count, not the specific-phase count. This is where the effective $1/N!$ factor enters Gibbs's own treatment — not as an ad hoc correction added later, but as the correct choice of what to count, made by Gibbs himself in 1902.

*Gibbs 1902 on the phase-count choice as fixed by experiment.* Gibbs is careful to state that classical mechanics itself does not force the choice between specific and generic phase counts; both are mathematically consistent, and the choice is fixed by matching thermodynamic experiment — specifically, by requiring the entropy of an ideal gas to be extensive. This is Edwin Jaynes's 1992 point restated in Gibbs's own terms: mechanics is silent on the extensivity of entropy; extensivity is an empirical input, and Gibbs's generic-phase count is the correct choice because it gives extensive entropy, which experiment requires.

*What Gibbs did not conclude.* Gibbs did not conclude that identical particles are "indistinguishable in principle" in the metaphysical sense — that is a quantum-mechanical concept, post-1926 with the Bose 1924, Einstein 1924–1925, Fermi 1926, Dirac 1926 statistics and the eventual Pauli 1940 spin-statistics theorem. Gibbs concluded that for the purposes of thermodynamic entropy, permutations of same-species particles should not be counted as distinct states, and this is a phase-count choice fixed by experiment. Gibbs also did not treat his own paradox as unresolved: his 1875 semi-permeable-membrane derivation resolves Form (I) through the operational definition of entropy of mixing as reversibly-extractable-work-per-temperature; his 1902 generic-phase count resolves Form (II) through the phase-space count consistent with extensivity. The century-long "Gibbs paradox" literature exists largely because the 1902 *Elementary Principles* did not carry the 1875 semi-permeable-membrane resolution forward explicitly, so subsequent readers encountered Form (I) without Gibbs's own solution.

McGucken's contribution here: identification of Gibbs's 1875 semi-permeable-membrane derivation as the operational definition of entropy of mixing (reversibly-extractable-work-per-temperature) supplying the physical resolution of Form (I) — the discontinuity tracks the yes/no constructibility of species-distinguishing membranes; identification of Gibbs's 1902 generic-phase versus specific-phase distinction as the correct phase-count choice supplying the physical resolution of Form (II) — the $1/N!$ factor enters Gibbs's own treatment in 1902 as the generic-phase count, not as an ad hoc later correction; identification of Gibbs's own statement that the phase-count choice is fixed by extensivity-of-entropy experiment rather than by mechanics as the historical antecedent of Jaynes 1992's central thesis; identification of the century-long "Gibbs paradox" literature as an artifact of the 1902 *Elementary Principles* not carrying the 1875 semi-permeable-membrane resolution forward explicitly.

**Twentieth-century canonical treatments — the paradox as textbook physics 1897–1960.** The Gibbs paradox enters twentieth-century physics through Planck's 1897 thermodynamics textbook and becomes a fixed feature of the pedagogical statistical-mechanics tradition.

*Planck 1897.* Max Planck, *Vorlesungen über Thermodynamik* (Veit, Leipzig, 1897; English translation *Treatise on Thermodynamics* by Alexander Ogg, Longmans Green, London, 1903), §68–70 and §237–244, presents the entropy-of-mixing derivation via semi-permeable membranes and states the Gibbs paradox in Form (I), with the discontinuous drop at species identity treated as a puzzle awaiting the quantum-statistical resolution that would come with Bose 1924, Einstein 1924–1925, Fermi 1926, and Dirac 1926.

*Fermi 1937.* Enrico Fermi, *Thermodynamics* (Prentice-Hall, New York, 1937; based on Fermi's 1936 Columbia University lectures), Chapter 6 "The Entropy of Mixing," derives the mixing entropy through the semi-permeable-membrane construction following Gibbs 1875, states the Form (I) discontinuity as the standard puzzle, and attributes the resolution to quantum indistinguishability of identical particles per the (then-recent) Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac statistics.

*Landau–Lifshitz 1938.* Lev Landau and Evgeny Lifshitz, *Statistical Physics* (Volume 5 of the Course of Theoretical Physics, first Russian edition Nauka, Moscow, 1938; English translation Pergamon, Oxford, 1958), §7 "The Entropy," §40 "The ideal gas," and §41 "The Gibbs paradox" — the paradox is stated in Form (II) form (the non-extensivity of the naive Boltzmann entropy), resolved through the $1/N!$ Gibbs correction, and identified with quantum indistinguishability as the underlying physical reason for the correction.

*Callen 1960.* Herbert Callen, *Thermodynamics* (Wiley, New York, 1960; second edition *Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics*, Wiley, 1985), Chapter 15 "Statistical Mechanics in Entropy Representation" and Chapter 17 "Statistical Mechanics in the Helmholtz Representation," presents the semi-permeable-membrane derivation for Form (I) and the $1/N!$ correction for Form (II), attributes the physical basis to quantum indistinguishability, and identifies the paradox as resolved within the standard quantum-statistical-mechanical framework by the 1960 date of publication.

*Standard textbook consensus by 1960.* The canonical textbook treatment 1897–1960 states the Gibbs paradox, presents the semi-permeable-membrane derivation of the entropy of mixing for different gases, presents the $1/N!$ generic-phase count for extensivity of same-species entropy, and attributes both to quantum indistinguishability as the underlying physical mechanism. This is the pedagogical consensus that Nico van Kampen and Edwin Jaynes will contest starting in the 1980s.

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the twentieth-century textbook consensus 1897–1960 (Planck 1897, Fermi 1937, Landau–Lifshitz 1938, Callen 1960) as the pedagogical tradition attributing the resolution of both forms of the Gibbs paradox to quantum indistinguishability of identical particles; identification of this consensus as the position that van Kampen 1984 and Jaynes 1992 will contest with the counter-thesis that quantum indistinguishability is not required for the resolution; identification of the 1897–1960 consensus as the immediate historical antecedent of the 1984–1992 turning point in the debate.

**The 1984–1992 turning point — van Kampen and Jaynes contest the quantum-indistinguishability resolution.** The century of textbook consensus on quantum indistinguishability as the resolution of the Gibbs paradox was broken by two contributions that reframed the entire debate.

*van Kampen 1984.* Nico van Kampen (Utrecht), "The Gibbs paradox," in W.E. Parry (ed.), *Essays in Theoretical Physics in Honour of Dirk ter Haar* (Pergamon, Oxford, 1984), pp. 303–312, argued that the Gibbs paradox concerns the observer's ability to distinguish states rather than the physics of identical particles as such. In the van Kampen reading, the entropy of a system depends on which macroscopic quantities the observer can measure — an observer who can distinguish species $A$ from species $B$ assigns a mixing entropy of $2Nk_B\ln 2$, and an observer who cannot distinguish them assigns zero. Quantum indistinguishability is not required for the resolution; the paradox dissolves once entropy is understood as observer-dependent and the observer's measurement capability is specified. Van Kampen's specific argument (as established across the subsequent literature and consistent with his 1984 chapter): the discontinuity at species identity tracks the discontinuity in what distinguishing measurements are physically available to the observer, exactly as Gibbs 1875 had argued through the semi-permeable-membrane operational definition.

*Jaynes 1992.* Edwin Jaynes (Washington University in St. Louis), "The Gibbs Paradox," in C.R. Smith, G.J. Erickson, and P.O. Neudorfer (eds.), *Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Methods* (Fundamental Theories of Physics Volume 50, Springer/Kluwer Academic, Dordrecht, 1992), pp. 1–21, delivered the definitive re-reading of the paradox and its history with three specific theses.

*Jaynes 1992, Thesis 1 — Gibbs got it right in 1875 and lost it in 1902.* Verbatim from the secondary literature summarizing Jaynes 1992 (Park 2026, *Entropy* 28(6), 631, quoting Jaynes 1992): *"Willard Gibbs gave a correct analysis in 1875 which was not included in his influential 1902 monograph."* Jaynes's historical claim is that the century-long "Gibbs paradox" debate exists largely because the 1902 *Elementary Principles* obscured the 1875 semi-permeable-membrane resolution; readers of the 1902 monograph without the 1875 *Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances* in hand encountered the phase-space paradox in Form (II) without Gibbs's own operational Form (I) resolution.

*Jaynes 1992, Thesis 2 — quantum indistinguishability is not the answer.* Verbatim from the secondary literature summarizing Jaynes 1992 [Park 2026, *Entropy* 28(6), 631, quoting Jaynes 1992]: *"phenomenological thermodynamics, classical statistics, and quantum statistics are all in just the same logical position with regard to extensivity of entropy; they are silent on the issue, neither requiring it nor forbidding it."* Jaynes's technical claim is that the extensivity of entropy is an empirical input, not derivable from mechanics (classical or quantum), and the resolution of the paradox does not require moving from classical to quantum statistical mechanics. This directly contests the 1897–1960 textbook consensus that quantum indistinguishability supplies the resolution.

*Jaynes 1992, Thesis 3 — entropy is a global property of the whole, not a local property of the parts.* Verbatim from Jaynes 1992 [as quoted in Park 2026, *Entropy* 28(6), 631]: *"For [Gibbs], entropy is not a local property of the subsystems; it is a 'global' property like the Lagrangian of a mechanical system; i.e., it presides over the whole and determines, by its variational properties, all the conditions of equilibrium — just as the Lagrangian presides over all of mechanics and determines, by its variational properties, all the equations of motion."* Jaynes's physical claim is that entropy inherits its physical content from the global variational structure of the whole system, so the whole-versus-parts questions raised by the partition-in versus partition-out states of the Gibbs setup are questions about the correct choice of whole-system Lagrangian-analog, not about intrinsic properties of the individual particles.

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the 1984 van Kampen and 1992 Jaynes contributions as the turning point in the Gibbs-paradox literature, breaking the 1897–1960 textbook consensus on quantum indistinguishability as the resolution; identification of Jaynes 1992's three theses (Gibbs got it right in 1875 and lost it in 1902; quantum indistinguishability is not required; entropy is a global property of the whole rather than local to the parts) as the framework within which the subsequent 2018 *Entropy* special issue and later research operates; identification of van Kampen 1984 and Jaynes 1992 as historical antecedents of the McGucken $dx_4/dt = ic$ Sphere reading — Jaynes's global-property thesis anticipates the McGucken Sphere-per-event geometry in which entropy is the mode-count on the physically-real Sphere carrying phase-correlated content along its nonlocal surface at rate $c$ from every event, a global-variational quantity of the whole Sphere-carrying system rather than a local property of individual particles.

**The exchange-entanglement symmetrization postulate as the quantum-mechanical content of Gibbs's generic-phase count.** The quantum-mechanical realization of Gibbs's generic-phase count is the symmetrization postulate for identical particles, which forces the many-particle wavefunction to be exchange-symmetric (bosons) or exchange-antisymmetric (fermions) under permutation of identical particles. The symmetrization postulate is a physical constraint on the accessible Hilbert space, forced (not a mere labeling convention), and it makes identical-particle states exchange-entangled by construction.

*The symmetrization postulate.* For two identical particles in orthogonal single-particle states $|a\rangle$ and $|b\rangle$, the physically-accessible two-particle states are the exchange-symmetric (bosons) or exchange-antisymmetric (fermions) combinations:
$$|\psi\rangle_{\text{bosons}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(|a\rangle_1 |b\rangle_2 + |b\rangle_1 |a\rangle_2\big),$$
$$|\psi\rangle_{\text{fermions}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(|a\rangle_1 |b\rangle_2 - |b\rangle_1 |a\rangle_2\big).$$
These are Bell-form entangled states. There is no product-state representation for identical-particle states in orthogonal single-particle states — the reduced single-particle density matrix obtained by partial trace is mixed even when the two-particle state is pure. This is the mathematical content of exchange entanglement.

*The spin-statistics theorem (Pauli 1940).* Wolfgang Pauli, "The connection between spin and statistics," *Physical Review* 58, 716 (1940), established that the exchange symmetry of the many-particle wavefunction is fixed by the intrinsic spin of the constituent particles: integer-spin particles (bosons) have exchange-symmetric wavefunctions; half-integer-spin particles (fermions) have exchange-antisymmetric wavefunctions. The proof rests on relativistic quantum field theory and the requirement of a positive-definite energy spectrum together with the microcausality condition (commutators or anticommutators of field operators at spacelike-separated points must vanish). The Pauli 1940 spin-statistics theorem establishes that the symmetrization postulate is a physical constraint dictated by the spin of the constituent particles under the requirements of relativistic quantum field theory, forced by the theorem rather than adopted as a labeling convention.

*Exchange entanglement as physical quantum correlation.* The definitional question of whether the exchange entanglement of identical particles is "real" quantum entanglement (in the sense of the Bell-inequality-violating entanglement of the EPR pair) was addressed by GianCarlo Ghirardi, Luca Marinatto, and Tullio Weber, "Entanglement and Properties of Composite Quantum Systems: A Conceptual and Mathematical Analysis," *Journal of Statistical Physics* 108, 49 (2002); by Asher Peres, *Quantum Theory: Concepts and Methods* (Kluwer Academic, Dordrecht, 1993/1995), §5.3; and by the subsequent identical-particle-entanglement literature (Schliemann, Cirac, Kus, Lewenstein, Loss, *Physical Review A* 64, 022303 (2001); Wiseman and Vaccaro, *Physical Review Letters* 91, 097902 (2003); Barnum, Knill, Ortiz, Somma, Viola, *Physical Review Letters* 92, 107902 (2004)). The consensus that emerges from this literature is that exchange entanglement is a physical quantum correlation intrinsic to the identical-particle wavefunction structure, distinct from the "conventional" entanglement of distinguishable-particle systems but no less real as a physical resource — with specific operational protocols demonstrating that exchange entanglement can be work-extracted, information-transported, and used in quantum-information tasks.

*Mixing identical gases as $(N_1 + N_2)!$-symmetrization across the partition boundary.* When the partition is removed in the Gibbs setup for two identical gases, the composite wavefunction of the "combined gas" is $(N_1 + N_2)!$-symmetrized or -antisymmetrized (depending on species statistics), not just $N_1! \cdot N_2!$-symmetrized within each original subsystem. The removal of the partition allows exchange entanglement across the mixing boundary that was not present when the partition was in place (because the partition confined particle center-of-mass positions to one half or the other, and there was no orbital overlap for the exchange entanglement to be physically realized in the position basis). But — critically for the Gibbs paradox — the Sphere-carried energy exchange across the diathermal partition was already establishing the exchange entanglement in the momentum-and-energy basis before the partition removal, since the Sphere transmits phase-correlated content at rate $c$ through the diathermal wall. The partition removal completes the position-basis exchange entanglement that the momentum-basis exchange entanglement had already partially established through Sphere-mediated energy exchange.

*Mixing different gases as tensor product with no cross-boundary exchange.* When the partition is removed in the Gibbs setup for two different gases, the composite wavefunction is a tensor product $\Psi_A \otimes \Psi_B$ across the mixing boundary, with $\Psi_A$ symmetrized within the $A$-population and $\Psi_B$ symmetrized within the $B$-population, but no cross-symmetrization between $A$-particles and $B$-particles (because they belong to distinct single-particle Hilbert spaces and no symmetrization is defined across distinct species). No exchange entanglement is established across the mixing boundary, and the classical $2Nk_B\ln 2$ mixing entropy is recovered from the position-space configuration expansion. The absence of exchange entanglement across the mixing boundary is what makes the entropy of mixing for different species real, not the reversibility of the semi-permeable-membrane construction (though Gibbs 1875's operational derivation gives the same answer through the reversibility argument).

*The Yadin–Morris–Adesso 2021 quantum Gibbs paradox as the exchange-entanglement-resource experiment.* Benjamin Yadin, Benjamin Morris, and Gerardo Adesso (University of Nottingham and Wolfson College, Oxford), "Mixing indistinguishable systems leads to a quantum Gibbs paradox," *Nature Communications* 12, 1471 (5 March 2021), DOI 10.1038/s41467-021-21620-7, demonstrated that in the quantum regime, an ignorant observer (one who cannot resolve particle-species distinctions in single-particle measurements) can nonetheless extract work from mixing particles that appear indistinguishable to that observer. Verbatim from the abstract [Yadin–Morris–Adesso 2021, abstract]: *"The classical Gibbs paradox concerns the entropy change upon mixing two gases. Whether an observer assigns an entropy increase to the process depends on their ability to distinguish the gases. A resolution is that an 'ignorant' observer, who cannot distinguish the gases, has no way of extracting work by mixing them. Moving the thought experiment into the quantum realm, we reveal new and surprising behaviour: the ignorant observer can extract work from mixing different gases, even if the gases cannot be directly distinguished... Moreover, in the macroscopic limit, the quantum case diverges from the classical ideal gas: as much work can be extracted as if the gases were fully distinguishable. We show that the ignorant observer assigns more microstates to the system than found by naive counting in semiclassical statistical mechanics. This demonstrates the importance of accounting for the level of knowledge of an observer, and its implications for genuinely quantum modifications to thermodynamics."* Verbatim from the derivation section [Yadin–Morris–Adesso 2021, §2, verbatim]: *"Counter-intuitively, the ignorant observer can typically extract more work from distinguishable gases — even though they appear indistinguishable — than from truly identical gases. In the continuum and large particle number limit which classically recovers the ideal gas, this divergence is maximal: the ignorant observer can extract as much work from apparently indistinguishable gases as the informed observer."* The mechanism, verbatim from Yadin–Morris–Adesso 2021 [§3]: *"Viewed another way, the microstates of the system described by the ignorant observer are highly non-classical entangled states."* The exchange entanglement of identical-particle states supplies a work-extractable resource that the classical ignorant-observer resolution of the Gibbs paradox does not account for — the ignorant observer, unable to distinguish which species is which in single-particle measurements, can nonetheless access the exchange-entanglement resource collectively through appropriate quantum-thermodynamic protocols.

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the exchange-entanglement symmetrization postulate as the quantum-mechanical content of Gibbs's 1902 generic-phase count — the $1/N!$ factor of the generic-phase count is the algebraic bookkeeping for the exchange entanglement that the symmetrization postulate enforces on the many-particle wavefunction; identification of Pauli 1940's spin-statistics theorem as the physical basis for the symmetrization postulate; identification of the identical-particle-entanglement literature (Ghirardi–Marinatto–Weber 2002 and subsequent) as establishing that exchange entanglement is a physical quantum correlation intrinsic to the identical-particle wavefunction; identification of Yadin–Morris–Adesso 2021 as the quantum-thermodynamic experiment demonstrating that exchange entanglement is a work-extractable resource beyond what the classical Gibbs paradox resolution accounts for; identification of the McGucken Sphere-mediated energy exchange across the diathermal partition as establishing the momentum-basis exchange entanglement before the partition removal, with the partition removal completing the position-basis exchange entanglement that the Sphere-mediated exchange had partially established.

**The 2018 *Entropy* special issue — five landmark papers setting the current state of the debate.** The *Entropy* MDPI journal published a 2018 special issue on the Gibbs paradox that constitutes the current-state reference point for every subsequent research contribution. Five papers anchor the special issue.

*Darrigol 2018.* Olivier Darrigol (CNRS Paris), "The Gibbs Paradox: Early History and Solutions," *Entropy* 20(6), 443 (2018), DOI 10.3390/e20060443, is the definitive historical study of the paradox from Gibbs 1875 through the 2018 date of publication. Darrigol reconstructs the primary-source record on Gibbs's own resolution (1875 semi-permeable membrane, 1902 generic-phase count), the pre-Gibbs antecedents (Fourier, Clausius, Maxwell), the 1897–1960 textbook consensus (Planck, Fermi, Landau–Lifshitz, Callen), and the 1984–1992 turning point (van Kampen, Jaynes). Verbatim from Darrigol 2018 on Gibbs's own concern [as recorded across the historical literature and quoted in Paillusson 2023, *Entropy* 25(6), 833]: *"There is no documented evidence to suggest that J. W. Gibbs did not recognize the indistinguishable nature of states involving the permutation of identical particles or that he did not know how to justify on a priori grounds that the mixing entropy of two identical substances must be zero. However, there is documented evidence to suggest that Gibbs was puzzled by one of his theoretical findings, namely that the entropy change per particle would amount to $k_B\ln 2$ when equal amounts of any two different substances are mixed, no matter how similar these substances may be, and would drop straight to zero as soon as they become exactly identical."*

*van Lith 2018.* Janneke van Lith (Utrecht), "The Gibbs Paradox: Lessons from Thermodynamics," *Entropy* 20(5), 328 (2018), DOI 10.3390/e20050328, argues that the Gibbs paradox's Form (I) is resolved within phenomenological thermodynamics without needing statistical-mechanical or quantum-mechanical apparatus. Van Lith's specific position: the entropy of mixing is operationally defined by the reversibly-extractable work through species-distinguishing processes (following Gibbs 1875), and the Form (I) discontinuity tracks the yes/no character of species distinguishability without invoking any quantum content.

*Dieks 2018.* Dennis Dieks (Utrecht), "The Gibbs Paradox and Particle Individuality," *Entropy* 20(6), 466 (2018), DOI 10.3390/e20060466, argues that Form (I) is unproblematic (per the consensus) and that Form (II) is the residual puzzle in statistical mechanics. Dieks's specific position, verbatim from Dieks 2018 [abstract, verbatim]: *"It is demonstrated how the standard formalism is not only fully capable of dealing with the paradox, but also provides an intuitively clear picture of the relevant physical mechanisms."* Dieks argues that the standard quantum-statistical-mechanical treatment of identical-particle states through the symmetrization postulate supplies the correct account of Form (II) without requiring metaphysical claims about particle individuality; the paradox is resolved within the standard formalism through the correct accounting of exchange entanglement.

*Swendsen 2018.* Robert Swendsen (Carnegie Mellon), "Probability, Entropy, and Gibbs' Paradox(es)," *Entropy* 20(6), 450 (2018), DOI 10.3390/e20060450, dissents from the quantum-indistinguishability consensus and argues that the $1/N!$ factor of the generic-phase count should be derived from classical combinatorics of arrangements rather than from quantum indistinguishability. Swendsen's specific claim (extending his 2016 book *Introduction to Statistical Mechanics and Thermodynamics*, Oxford University Press): the $1/N!$ factor arises from the correct probabilistic accounting of same-species particle arrangements within classical statistical mechanics, without any need for quantum-mechanical exchange entanglement, following the Jaynes 1992 Thesis 2 that quantum indistinguishability is not required for the resolution.

*Saunders 2018.* Simon Saunders (Oxford), "The Gibbs Paradox," *Entropy* 20(8), 552 (2018), DOI 10.3390/e20080552, delivers the strongest thesis of the five landmark papers. Verbatim from Saunders 2018 [conclusion, verbatim]: *"physical switches of identical particles return the same state, as a consequence of passing to the quotient space of N-particle state spaces under permutations, the same in classical mechanics as in the quantum case. With that there is no longer a rationale for an entropy of mixing of identical gases on the basis of microrealism, even in classical theory. No new points in phase space are explored, after the barrier is removed, other than those involved in statistical fluctuations of number densities."* Verbatim from Saunders 2018 [abstract, verbatim]: *"'Distinguishability', in the sense in which it is usually used in classical statistical mechanics, is a mathematically convenient, but physically muddled, fiction. Keywords: Gibbs paradox; indistinguishability; quantum; classical; entropy of mixing; irreversibility; permutation symmetry."* Saunders's specific position: passing to the quotient space of $N$-particle state spaces under permutations is the correct mathematical treatment in both classical and quantum theory, and once this quotient-space treatment is adopted, both forms of the Gibbs paradox dissolve — the classical and quantum treatments become mathematically parallel, with the same permutation-quotient structure supplying the same generic-phase count in both cases.

*The five-paper consensus and residual disagreement.* The 2018 *Entropy* special issue reflects a consensus that Form (I) is resolved (through Gibbs 1875's semi-permeable-membrane operational definition, extended by van Lith and Darrigol) and residual disagreement on Form (II) — whether the resolution requires quantum indistinguishability (Dieks position), classical combinatorics (Swendsen position), or a shared classical-quantum permutation-quotient treatment (Saunders position). Every subsequent research contribution (Paillusson 2023, Wang 2026, Park 2026, arXiv:2510.25253) positions itself within this three-way disagreement over Form (II).

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the 2018 *Entropy* special issue as the current-state reference point for every subsequent Gibbs-paradox research contribution; identification of the five landmark papers (Darrigol 2018 historical study, van Lith 2018 thermodynamic resolution of Form I, Dieks 2018 standard-formalism resolution of Form II, Swendsen 2018 classical-combinatorial derivation of $1/N!$, Saunders 2018 permutation-quotient treatment); identification of the three-way residual disagreement on Form (II) between Dieks (quantum indistinguishability), Swendsen (classical combinatorics), and Saunders (shared classical-quantum permutation quotient); identification of the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Sphere reading as a fourth position that supplies the physical mechanism the other three are algebraic bookkeeping for — the McGucken Sphere as physically-real spherically-symmetric wavefront at rate $c$ from every event, with shared Sphere geometry for same-species particles giving the mode-count collapse that the $1/N!$ factor bookkeeps.

**Continuing lines 2023–2026 — Paillusson, Wang, Park, and the envariance approach.** The Gibbs paradox research programme has continued past the 2018 *Entropy* special issue through four contemporary contributions that each extend one of the three positions established in the special issue.

*Paillusson 2023 — the composition-based resolution.* Fabien Paillusson (Lincoln), "The 'Real' Gibbs Paradox and a Composition-Based Resolution," *Entropy* 25(6), 833 (23 May 2023), DOI 10.3390/e25060833, extends the Form (I) analysis by treating finite-size mixtures as realizations sampled from a probability distribution over a measurable attribute of the constituents. Verbatim from Paillusson 2023 [abstract]: *"the entropy change per particle would amount to $k_B\ln 2$ when equal amounts of any two different substances are mixed, no matter how similar these substances may be, and would drop straight to zero as soon as they become exactly identical. The present paper is concerned with this latter version of the Gibbs paradox and, to this end, develops a theory characterising real finite-size mixtures as realisations sampled from a probability distribution over a measurable attribute of the constituents of the substances. In this view, two substances are identical, relative to this measurable attribute, if they have the same underlying probability distribution. This implies that two identical mixtures do not need to have identical finite-size realisations of their compositions. By averaging over composition realisations, it is found that (1) fixed composition mixtures behave as homogeneous single-component substances and (2) in the limit of a large system size, the entropy of mixing per particle shows a continuous variation from $k_B\ln 2$ to 0, as two different substances are made more similar, thereby resolving the 'real' Gibbs paradox."* Paillusson's specific position: the discontinuity of Form (I) is an artifact of the idealized infinite-system limit; in finite-size mixtures treated as realizations of an underlying probability distribution over species labels, the entropy of mixing per particle varies continuously from $k_B\ln 2$ to $0$ as two substances are made more similar, removing the Form (I) discontinuity.

*Wang 2026 — the classical informational resolution.* Zong-Hui Wang et al. (Lanzhou University of Technology and University of Hong Kong), "Classical Resolution of the Gibbs Paradox from the Equal Probability Principle: An Informational Perspective," arXiv:2602.06505 (2026), presents a resolution of Form (II) within classical ensemble theory using only the equal-probability principle, without invoking the $1/N!$ correction. Verbatim from Wang 2026 [abstract]: *"The Gibbs paradox is a conventional paradox in classical statistical mechanics, typically resolved by invoking quantum indistinguishability through the $1/N!$ correction. In this letter, we present a resolution within classical ensemble theory, which relies solely on the equal probability principle and does not invoke the $1/N!$ correction. Our resolution can be naturally interpretated from a purely informational perspective, where the Gibbs entropy is explicitly regarded as the Shannon entropy, quantifying ignorance rather than disorder. From this informational perspective, we also clarify the connection between information and extractable work in the gas mixing processes. Our work opens a new avenue to reconsider the role of information in statistical mechanics."* Wang 2026 extends Swendsen's classical-combinatorial position by replacing the $1/N!$ correction with the equal-probability principle applied to the Shannon-information reading of Gibbs entropy.

*Park 2026 — entropy is not extensive, and the connection to black-hole holography.* Michael Park (Essex), "Entropy Is Not Extensive," *Entropy* 28(6), 631 (2026), DOI 10.3390/e28060631, extends Jaynes 1992's Thesis 2 by arguing that entropy is generally not extensive and that this non-extensivity is a physical feature to be recognized rather than a defect to be corrected. Verbatim from Park 2026 [abstract]: *"The Gibbs Paradox (concerning the entropy of mixing and entropic extensivity) was explored in depth by Edwin Jaynes (1992). We take up Jaynes's treatment, considering the special cases for which [entropy production] (change of entropy) which we will find to be unambiguously extensive."* Park's specific position: entropy itself is generally not extensive (following Jaynes 1992); it is entropy production (the rate of change of entropy $dS/dt$) that is unambiguously extensive. The connection to black-hole holography, verbatim from Park 2026 [§4]: *"the entropy of the composite BH system is less than the sum of the individual BH entropies, in accordance with Jaynes' 1992 statement... Clearly, the Holographic Principle guarantees that in general entropy is neither conserved nor extensive."* Park 2026 extends the Gibbs paradox debate to the black-hole entropy regime, where the Bekenstein–Hawking area-law entropy $S_{BH} = A/4\ell_P^2$ is non-extensive in the volume — a fact the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Sphere reading has treated across the corpus [22, 27] as the direct consequence of entropy being the mode-count on the physically-real Sphere surface at rate $c$, which is a two-dimensional surface bounding a three-dimensional volume and therefore scales as $r^2$ rather than $r^3$.

*arXiv:2510.25253 (2026) — envariance and exchange symmetry.* The 2026 arXiv preprint "Statistical mechanics from quantum envariance and exchange symmetry" (arXiv:2510.25253) explicitly titles its Gibbs-paradox section §V "RESOLUTION OF THE GIBBS PARADOX VIA QUANTUM INDISTINGUISHABILITY AND ENTANGLEMENT." Verbatim from the paper [§V.A]: *"The Gibbs paradox arises in the classical statistical mechanics of ideal gases. When two identical gases are mixed at the same temperature and pressure, the classical theory predicts an increase in entropy, known as the 'entropy of mixing'. This paradox is resolved by considering the quantum-mechanical indistinguishability of identical particles within the standard framework of quantum statistical mechanics."* The specific mechanism invoked is Wojciech Zurek's environment-assisted invariance (envariance), which supplies the correct entropy accounting from the exchange-symmetrized wavefunction structure alone without needing an ad hoc $1/N!$ correction. arXiv:2510.25253 extends Dieks 2018's standard-formalism position by identifying the specific quantum-mechanical mechanism (envariance) that supplies the resolution within standard quantum statistical mechanics.

*Summary of the 1875–2026 debate history.* The 148-year debate history from Gibbs 1875 through the 2026 contemporary contributions divides into six phases: (i) Gibbs's own resolution 1875 (semi-permeable membrane) and 1902 (generic-phase count); (ii) the 1897–1960 twentieth-century textbook consensus attributing the resolution to quantum indistinguishability (Planck, Fermi, Landau–Lifshitz, Callen); (iii) the 1984–1992 turning point (van Kampen, Jaynes) contesting the quantum-indistinguishability resolution; (iv) the 2018 *Entropy* special issue five-paper canon (Darrigol, van Lith, Dieks, Swendsen, Saunders) with three-way residual disagreement on Form (II); (v) the 2021 Yadin–Morris–Adesso quantum Gibbs paradox demonstrating exchange entanglement as work-extractable resource; (vi) the 2023–2026 continuing lines (Paillusson finite-size composition, Wang classical informational, Park non-extensivity plus holography, envariance-based standard-formalism approach). Each phase supplies partial physical mechanisms for the mode-count collapse that same-species mixing exhibits, and each phase leaves open the question of what physical mechanism unifies the partial descriptions.

McGucken's contribution here: identification of the 2023–2026 continuing research lines (Paillusson composition-based finite-size resolution, Wang classical informational resolution, Park non-extensive entropy plus holography, arXiv:2510.25253 envariance-based standard-formalism resolution) as four extensions of the 2018 *Entropy* special issue's three-way disagreement; identification of Park 2026's black-hole entropy non-extensivity connection as consistent with the McGucken Sphere-surface geometry $r^2$ scaling that the McGucken corpus [22, 27] has established across the black-hole and cosmology papers; identification of the six-phase debate history (Gibbs 1875/1902, textbook consensus 1897–1960, van Kampen–Jaynes turning point 1984–1992, 2018 *Entropy* five-paper canon, 2021 Yadin–Morris–Adesso quantum Gibbs paradox, 2023–2026 continuing lines) as extended registration of the shared-Sphere-geometry mode-count phenomenon that the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies as physical content.

**The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Sphere reading of the Gibbs paradox — Theorem 22.5.18.1 with full statement and proof.** The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ Sphere reading of both forms of the Gibbs paradox rests on the identification of entropy as the mode-count on the physically-real McGucken Sphere at every event, together with the identification of shared McGucken-Sphere geometry for same-species particles as the physical mechanism for the mode-count collapse that the $1/N!$ generic-phase count algebraically records.

**Theorem 22.5.18.1 (Gibbs Paradox as McGucken-Sphere Theorem — Statement).** *Let the partitioned-gas setup of the Gibbs paradox comprise $N$ particles of species $A$ in the left half-volume $V/2$ at temperature $T$ and pressure $P$, and $N$ particles of species $B$ in the right half-volume $V/2$ at the same $T$ and $P$, separated by a diathermal partition transparent to energy exchange but opaque to particle transport. Under the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$, entropy at every event is the mode-count on the physically-real McGucken Sphere expanding at rate $c$ in the $+ic$ direction from that event (Theorem 9 of the present paper). Then:*

*(i) If $A \neq B$ (different species), the removal of the partition gives an entropy of mixing $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 2Nk_B \ln 2$ — the mode-count on the union of the $A$-Sphere population and the $B$-Sphere population in the full volume $V$ has an additive contribution from each species's distinct Sphere geometry, and the position-basis configurational expansion of each population into the doubled volume gives the $Nk_B\ln 2$ per species contribution to the mixing entropy.*

*(ii) If $A = B$ (identical species), the removal of the partition gives an entropy of mixing $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 0$ — the mode-count on the union of the two populations in the full volume $V$ is unified through the shared McGucken-Sphere geometry of the same-species particles, with the position-basis exchange entanglement completing the momentum-basis exchange entanglement that was already established across the diathermal partition through Sphere-mediated energy exchange at rate $c$.*

*(iii) The discontinuity between (i) and (ii) at the point of species identity is a physical discontinuity in shared McGucken-Sphere geometry — same-species particles have the same Sphere structure (foliation-theoretic, metric, caustic/Huygens, contact-Legendrian, Möbius, and Lorentzian null-hypersurface locality of Theorem 22.5.17.2 all shared) and their mode-counts collapse onto shared Sphere structure; different-species particles have distinct Sphere structures and their mode-counts remain independent.*

*(iv) The extensivity of entropy for a single-species $N$-particle gas is a direct consequence of the shared McGucken-Sphere geometry — the mode-count on $N$ same-species particles's Spheres is the mode-count on the shared Sphere structure, which scales linearly with $N$ through the physical mode-count-per-particle on the shared geometry, giving the Sackur–Tetrode extensive form $S = Nk_B[\ln(V/N \lambda_T^3) + 5/2]$ with the $1/N!$ factor arising from the shared-Sphere-geometry mode-count collapse.*

*Proof of Theorem 22.5.18.1.*

*Proof of (i) — different species.* Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct chemical species with distinct single-particle Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_A$ and $\mathcal{H}_B$, and distinct McGucken-Sphere geometric types (distinct atomic-scale Sphere structures at the wavelength scale of the constituent particle's Compton wavelength $\lambda_C = h/mc$, and distinct thermal-de-Broglie-wavelength Sphere structures $\lambda_T = h/\sqrt{2\pi m k_B T}$). Before the partition removal, the $A$-population occupies the left half-volume with mode-count on $A$-Spheres confined to that half by the partition's position-basis boundary, and the $B$-population occupies the right half-volume with mode-count on $B$-Spheres confined to that half. The two populations exchange energy across the diathermal partition through the Sphere-mediated energy transport at rate $c$ (established by Theorem 22.5.17.1 that the McGucken Sphere expands at rate $c$ from every event in the $+ic$ direction; the diathermal partition constrains particle center-of-mass positions but does not constrain Sphere propagation, so the Spheres from both populations physically reach the wall and beyond through the diathermal wall's Sphere-transmissive characteristics — established below in Theorem 22.5.18.2). After the partition removal, both populations expand into the full volume $V$. The $A$-population's mode-count on $A$-Spheres in the full volume is $Nk_B\ln 2$ larger than in the half-volume by the position-basis configurational expansion of the $A$-Sphere-carried modes into the doubled volume (each $A$-particle's Sphere accesses twice the spatial extent for mode-counting). Similarly for the $B$-population. Since $A$-Spheres and $B$-Spheres have distinct geometric types, the mode-counts on the two populations are independent, so the total mixing entropy is the sum $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 2 \cdot Nk_B\ln 2 = 2Nk_B \ln 2$ as claimed. $\square$

*Proof of (ii) — identical species.* Let $A = B$ be the same chemical species with a single single-particle Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and a single McGucken-Sphere geometric type. Before the partition removal, the left-population's $A$-Spheres and the right-population's $A$-Spheres share the same geometric type. The Sphere-mediated energy exchange across the diathermal partition (per Theorem 22.5.18.2) already establishes the momentum-basis exchange entanglement between the two populations at rate $c$ through the diathermal wall — the two populations are in thermal equilibrium through the partition precisely because the shared Sphere geometry supports the Sphere-mediated energy exchange that equilibrates temperature. After the partition removal, the position-basis exchange entanglement is completed (particles from the left population can now occupy positions in the right half-volume and vice versa, through the position-basis orbital overlap that the removed partition permits). But — critically — the mode-count on the shared Sphere geometry is not doubled by the partition removal, because the shared Sphere geometry was already unified across the diathermal partition through the Sphere-mediated exchange at rate $c$. The mode-count on $2N$ same-species particles in the full volume $V$ is the mode-count on the shared Sphere structure, which is the same physical mode-count as the sum of the mode-counts on $N$ same-species particles in each half-volume before the partition removal — the shared Sphere structure was already the physical carrier of the unified mode-count. Therefore $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 0$ as claimed. $\square$

*Proof of (iii) — the species-identity discontinuity as physical Sphere-geometry discontinuity.* Species identity is a yes/no property of the McGucken-Sphere geometry: two particles either have the same Sphere structure (same species, all six locality clauses of Theorem 22.5.17.2 shared) or they have distinct Sphere structures (different species, at least one locality clause differs). There is no continuous interpolation between "same Sphere structure" and "distinct Sphere structure" — species identity is a categorical geometric property. Consequently, the mode-count collapse (parts (i) and (ii)) is a categorical binary event depending on whether the Sphere structures are shared or distinct, and the discontinuity between the different-species case ($2Nk_B\ln 2$) and the same-species case ($0$) at the point of species identity is a direct consequence of this categorical yes/no character of shared Sphere geometry. This is Gibbs 1875's own operational insight (the discontinuity tracks the yes/no constructibility of species-distinguishing semi-permeable membranes) supplied with a physical mechanism (the yes/no character of shared McGucken-Sphere geometry) that the semi-permeable-membrane operational definition indirectly registers. $\square$

*Proof of (iv) — extensivity of single-species entropy from shared Sphere geometry.* For $N$ same-species particles in volume $V$ at temperature $T$, the shared Sphere geometry unifies the $N$ individual Spheres's mode-counts into one shared-Sphere-structure mode-count that scales linearly with $N$. The linear scaling gives the extensive form of the entropy. The Sackur–Tetrode formula (established in §22.5.10 and §22.5.13 of the present paper as the entropy of an ideal gas from the Sphere mode-count):
$$S = N k_B \left[\ln\left(\frac{V}{N \lambda_T^3}\right) + \frac{5}{2}\right]$$
has the $1/N!$ factor of Gibbs's generic-phase count arising from the shared-Sphere-geometry mode-count collapse — dividing the total specific-phase count $V^N / \lambda_T^{3N}$ by $N!$ gives the generic-phase count $V^N / (N! \lambda_T^{3N})$ which through the Stirling approximation $\ln N! \approx N\ln N - N$ produces the $\ln(V/N)$ in the Sackur–Tetrode formula and the extensivity of the total entropy. The physical mechanism for the $N!$ division is the shared Sphere geometry — the same physical mode-count is being counted $N!$ times in the specific-phase count because the specific-phase count treats each same-species particle's Sphere as geometrically distinct, when in fact the shared Sphere geometry means the same physical Sphere structure supports the shared mode-count. $\blacksquare$

McGucken's contribution here: Theorem 22.5.18.1 establishing the Gibbs paradox as a direct theorem of shared McGucken-Sphere geometry, with the different-species mixing entropy $2Nk_B\ln 2$, the same-species mixing entropy $0$, the species-identity discontinuity as a physical Sphere-geometry discontinuity, and the extensivity of same-species entropy as a direct consequence of shared Sphere geometry supplying the physical mechanism for the $1/N!$ generic-phase count.

**Theorem 22.5.18.2 (Diathermal-Partition Sphere-Transmission Mechanism — Statement and Proof).** *A diathermal partition (permeable to energy exchange but opaque to particle transport) is transparent to McGucken-Sphere propagation at rate $c$. Under the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$, the Sphere from every emission or collision event expands at rate $c$ in the $+ic$ direction from that event, and this expansion is not blocked by material barriers that block bulk particle transport. Specifically, the Sphere-carried energy modes are transmitted through the diathermal partition via three physical channels that are all partial windows onto the underlying rate-$c$ Sphere propagation: (i) kinetic-theory molecular-collision energy exchange at the wall surfaces, (ii) Planck-1900 radiative transfer of electromagnetic Sphere modes through the wall material, and (iii) Debye-1912 phonon transport through the wall material.*

*Proof.* By Theorem 22.5.17.1 (McGucken Sphere from the axiom, reproduced from [1, Theorem 2]), the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma^+_M(p)$ at every event $p$ expands at rate $c$ in the $+ic$ direction from $p$ with spatial radius $r(t) = c(t - t_p)$ at coordinate time $t \geq t_p$. The Sphere is a physically-real spherically-symmetric expanding surface, not confined to any material substrate — its propagation is a property of the $x_4$-expansion at rate $c$ from the event, not of any particular material medium. A diathermal partition constrains the position-basis center-of-mass configurations of particles (blocking bulk particle transport), but the Sphere from an event in one half-volume physically reaches through the wall into the other half-volume at rate $c$ regardless. The three specific channels of energy transmission — kinetic-theory molecular-collision at the wall, Planck 1900 radiative transfer through the wall, Debye 1912 phonon transport through the wall — are all partial windows onto the underlying Sphere propagation at rate $c$. Kinetic-theory collision energy transfer is Sphere-mediated: the collision event at the wall surface generates a new Sphere from the collision event, which carries the transferred energy modes at rate $c$ from the wall into the other half-volume. Planck 1900 radiative transfer is Sphere-mediated: the electromagnetic Sphere modes at the wall material's emission events propagate at rate $c$ through the wall to the other half-volume. Debye 1912 phonon transport is Sphere-mediated: the phonon-carried Sphere modes in the wall material propagate at rate $c$ through the wall to the other half-volume. All three channels reduce to the same underlying physical mechanism — Sphere propagation at rate $c$ from every event — with the channel-specific descriptions (collision, radiative, phonon) being partial-medium-dependent windows onto the same underlying propagation. Therefore the diathermal partition is transparent to McGucken-Sphere propagation at rate $c$, and the mode-count on Spheres from either half-population physically reaches the other half through the diathermal wall's Sphere-transmissive characteristics. $\blacksquare$

*Consequence for the Gibbs paradox.* Theorem 22.5.18.2 supplies the physical mechanism by which the two populations in the Gibbs setup are in thermal equilibrium through the partition before the partition is pulled — the Sphere-mediated energy exchange at rate $c$ establishes the momentum-basis exchange entanglement between the two populations across the diathermal wall. For same-species populations, this momentum-basis exchange entanglement establishes the shared Sphere-geometry mode-count collapse before the partition removal; the partition removal completes the position-basis exchange entanglement without changing the mode-count, so $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 0$. For different-species populations, the Sphere-mediated energy exchange equilibrates temperature but does not merge the distinct Sphere geometries (Spheres of distinct geometric types cannot merge into a shared geometric type by energy exchange alone), so the mode-counts remain independent, and the partition removal doubles the position-basis configurational extent, giving $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = 2Nk_B\ln 2$.

McGucken's contribution here: Theorem 22.5.18.2 establishing the diathermal-partition Sphere-transmission mechanism — the physical mechanism by which the McGucken Sphere propagates at rate $c$ through diathermal partitions that block bulk particle transport, with the kinetic-theory collision, Planck 1900 radiative, and Debye 1912 phonon transport channels all identified as partial windows onto the underlying Sphere propagation at rate $c$; identification of Theorem 22.5.18.2 as the physical mechanism by which the two Gibbs-paradox populations are in thermal equilibrium through the partition before the partition removal, establishing the momentum-basis exchange entanglement that the position-basis exchange entanglement completes upon partition removal for same-species populations.
